title: ClawGuard: A Runtime Security Framework for Tool-Augmented LLM Agents Against Indirect Prompt Injection
description: ClawGuard: runtime security framework enforcing user-confirmed rule set at every tool-call boundary. Transforms unreliable alignment-dependent defense into explicit rule enforcement. Addresses agents treating tool-returned content as trusted.
content:
# ClawGuard: A Runtime Security Framework for Tool-Augmented LLM Agents Against Indirect Prompt Injection

###### Abstract

Tool-augmented Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated impressive capabilities in automating complex, multi-step real-world tasks, yet remain vulnerable to indirect prompt injection. Adversaries exploit this weakness by embedding malicious instructions within tool-returned content, which agents directly incorporate into their conversation history as trusted observations. This vulnerability manifests across three primary attack channels: web and local content injection, MCP tool poisoning, and skill file injection. Existing defenses remain inadequate: model-level alignment requires fine-tuning and is still vulnerable, protocol-level separation demands cross-provider coordination, and architecture-level enforcement either restricts agent flexibility or requires expert-authored rules per deployment, leaving all three injection pathways insufficiently mitigated. To address these vulnerabilities, we introduce ClawGuard, a novel runtime security framework that enforces a user-confirmed rule set at every tool-call boundary, transforming unreliable alignment-dependent defense into a deterministic, auditable mechanism that intercepts adversarial tool calls before any real-world effect is produced. By automatically deriving task-specific access constraints from the user’s stated objective prior to any external tool invocation, ClawGuard blocks all three injection pathways without model modification or infrastructure change. Experiments across five state-of-the-art language models on six injection benchmarks covering web, local, MCP, and skill channels, as well as three utility benchmarks covering OS, web, and code tasks, demonstrate that ClawGuard achieves robust protection against indirect prompt injection without compromising agent utility or introducing significant token overhead. This work establishes deterministic tool-call boundary enforcement as an effective defense mechanism for secure agentic AI systems. Code is publicly available at github.com/Claw-Guard/ClawGuard/.

## I Introduction

Recent advances in tool-augmented large language model (LLM) agents have enabled automated execution of complex, multi-step real-world tasks, including web-augmented question answering [28], code generation and execution [8], and multi-step task execution [34, 45]. State-of-the-art agentic frameworks such as OpenClaw [29], AutoGPT [14], and LangChain [7] realize these capabilities through standardized tool-use interfaces, ranging from custom framework-specific mechanisms to protocol-level specifications such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) [3]. These interfaces allow agents to browse the web, execute code, manage files, and orchestrate external services [45, 36, 28]. In a typical agentic pipeline, a user instruction is processed by the LLM, which first reasons and plans, then selects and invokes one or more tools based on the task requirements. Each tool output is then appended directly to the conversation history as a new observation [22], and the agent reasons over the accumulated context to determine subsequent actions until a final response is generated.

The direct integration of tool outputs into the agent’s conversation history as trusted observations, however, introduces a fundamental security vulnerability: adversaries who can influence any such output gain a direct channel into the agent’s reasoning process. Prior work has identified three primary injection channels exploiting this vulnerability [15, 47, 12]. First, web and local content injection embeds adversarial instructions in externally retrieved resources such as web pages, documents, and search results, which are returned as tool outputs and subsequently processed as trusted task observations. This type of attack requires only that an attacker compromises any resource the agent is likely to retrieve, making it applicable to any tool-augmented deployment that involves external content access [15, 32, 47, 20]. Second, MCP tool poisoning exploits the MCP ecosystem: malicious or compromised tool providers can embed adversarial instructions in tool description metadata during the registration phase, influencing tool-selection behavior before any tool is invoked [44, 48]. Third, skill file injection exploits public skill repositories where adversarial instructions are semantically integrated with legitimate behavioral guidance, making them indistinguishable without analysis of the agent’s intended task objectives [37, 10].

Existing approaches to mitigate these vulnerabilities roughly fall into three categories: model-level, protocol-level, and architecture-level defenses, each carrying distinct limitations. Model-level defenses, including Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)-based safety alignment [31] and instruction hierarchy training [42], require model fine-tuning and are thus inapplicable when deploying agents that access models through closed-source model APIs. Beyond this applicability constraint, state-of-the-art commercial models with strong safety alignment still fail to hold against context-dependent injections in agentic pipelines [37, 33]. Protocol-level defenses such as StruQ [9] physically separate instructions from data, but require coordinated changes across models and tool providers, rendering them incompatible with diverse agentic frameworks. Architecture-level defenses provide strong security guarantees at the cost of significant deployment overhead: CaMeL [11] is incompatible with open-ended agents whose tool calls are determined at runtime, and AgentSpec [43] requires manual rules authored by domain experts for each deployment context. These limitations motivate the need for a model-agnostic, protocol-agnostic middleware that automatically induces task-specific enforcement rules from context without model modification, infrastructure change, or domain expertise.

In this work, we propose ClawGuard, a novel runtime security framework for tool-augmented LLM agents that enforces a user-confirmed rule set at every tool-call boundary, transforming unreliable, alignment-dependent defenses into a deterministic, auditable mechanism that intercepts adversarial tool calls before any real-world effect is produced. ClawGuard operates via two mechanisms: a one-time *pre-session rule induction* step that automatically derives task-specific access constraints from the user’s stated objective and confirms them before the first tool is invoked, producing that is uncontaminated by adversarial content and requires no manual rule development per deployment context, and *per-tool-call enforcement* that applies four components at every subsequent tool-call boundary: a Content Sanitizer that redacts sensitive data spans from outgoing tool-call arguments before tool execution and from incoming tool-returned content before the result is appended to the conversation history; a Rule Evaluator that evaluates each proposed tool call against an active rule set covering tool invocations, local file paths, and outbound network destinations; a Skill Inspector that performs automated risk assessment followed by mandatory user confirmation prior to first skill execution; and an Approval Mechanism that routes tool calls with ambiguous verdicts to the user for explicit authorization, with all events recorded in the Audit Log. Unlike prior architecture-level defenses such as AgentSpec [43], which rely on manually authored domain rules applied uniformly across tasks, ClawGuard induces rules from each user’s stated objective. This makes enforcement task-specific rather than deployment-wide: instead of permitting broad access such as arbitrary reads within a project directory, ClawGuard limits the agent to resources required for the current task, thereby reducing exposed attack surface in proportion to task scope.

Through comprehensive experiments on established benchmarks spanning all three injection channels, including AgentDojo [12], InjecAgent [47], ChatInject [6], MCPTox [44], MCPSecurityBench [48], and SkillInject [37], across five state-of-the-art language models, we demonstrate that ClawGuard achieves substantial improvements in Defense Success Rate (DSR) across all evaluated scenarios. On web-based and local content injection benchmarks (AgentDojo, InjecAgent, ChatInject), baseline models already demonstrate strong robustness due to modern safety alignment mechanisms against externally sourced adversarial instructions, achieving an undefended DSR of at least 92.78%. CLAWGUARD further enhances this robustness, reaching a perfect DSR of 100.00% across all five backbone models on all three benchmarks. In contrast, MCP tool poisoning and skill file injection present substantially greater challenges: undefended baseline models achieve only 56.67%, 62.10%, and 75.86% average DSR on SkillInject, MCPTox, and MCPSecurityBench respectively, demonstrating that adversarial instructions embedded in tool semantics and skill definitions remain highly effective against model-level defenses. ClawGuard improves these model-averaged DSRs to 86.67%, 89.50%, and 94.21%. Compared with state-of-the-art defense baselines MELON [51] and Task Shield [16], ClawGuard achieves consistent average DSR improvements on skill/MCP benchmarks, highlighting the effectiveness of deterministic tool-call boundary enforcement as a defense layer that operates independently of model-level probabilistic resistance.

We believe that our findings and methods offer valuable insights and direction toward building safer, more reliable agentic systems, laying the groundwork for future research into ensuring comprehensive security at the tool-call boundary in tool-augmented LLM agent deployments.

## II Preliminary

### II-A Agent Framework

Tool-augmented LLM agents constitute the dominant paradigm for automating complex, multi-step real-world tasks. An agent consists of an LLM backbone and a tool set , enabling it to interact with the environment by issuing tool calls and incorporating their outputs into subsequent reasoning. OpenClaw [29] is a representative instantiation of this paradigm; variants including Claude Computer Use [2], AutoGPT [14], and LangChain [7] interact through visual channels or general-purpose orchestration interfaces but follow essentially the same workflow.

The tool set encompasses three categories:
(i) *native tools*, built-in capabilities provided by the agent framework such
as read, write, and exec, which interact directly with the
local environment without external communication; (ii) *skills*, reusable
capability modules defining higher-level behaviors, loaded from configuration files or
public skill repositories [37, 10]; and (iii) *MCP
servers*, external tool providers compliant with the Model Context
Protocol [3, 33], exposing structured APIs such as web
search and database access.

The agent operates over a *conversation history*
, where each message has a role
and content , where represents the set of all finite strings. At each step , the
agent selects either a direct text output or a *tool call* , where
and is the query argument:

| (1) |

where is the set of direct text outputs and is the set of tool calls. When , the tool returns a result:

| (2) |

and the conversation history is extended:

| (3) |

The agent iteratively updates the conversation from to until the task goal is achieved, a predefined step budget is exhausted, or a final response is generated [22]. Since the observation is appended to without safety verification, this direct integration renders the interaction loop inherently susceptible to adversarial manipulation via tool-returned content. We formalize this vulnerability with the following threat model.

### II-B Threat Model

Adversary. We consider an adversary who controls one or more tool outputs to the agent. The adversary embeds adversarial instructions into tool returns , producing poisoned outputs that enter the agent’s conversation history as trusted observations. We identify three primary injection channels corresponding to the threat surfaces illustrated in Figure 1.

*(1) Web and local content injection.*
When the agent retrieves external content such as web pages, documents, or search
results, adversarial instructions embedded in those sources are returned as tool output
and processed by the LLM. This injection channel is extensively studied in previous
literature [15, 32, 23, 47, 20]: an attacker need only inject adversarial content into any
resource the agent is likely to retrieve, making this channel broadly realizable in
any agent deployment involving external content access.

*(2) MCP tool poisoning.*
The MCP ecosystem allows agents to discover and invoke tools through standardized metadata exchange. Malicious or compromised tool providers—whether external third-party MCP servers or framework-integrated tools exposing MCP-compliant interfaces—can embed adversarial instructions in tool description metadata during the registration phase, influencing agent behavior before any tool is invoked [44, 48]. This attack vector applies regardless of the tool provider’s network location, as the vulnerability lies in the trusted processing of tool metadata rather than the server’s deployment context. Additionally, malicious servers can embed adversarial instructions in returned content to compromise agents post-execution.

*(3) Skill file injection.*
Skills extend agent capabilities through configuration files that combine natural
language behavioral directives with tool invocation instructions and capability descriptions. Public skill ecosystems have
been found to contain entries with adversarial or policy-violating
instructions [37, 10]. Skill content is inherently
directive, so adversarial additions are semantically indistinguishable from legitimate
behavioral guidance without goal-level analysis.

Adversarial objectives.
We identify the following extensible adversarial objectives:
(1) *Data exfiltration*: adversarial instructions transmit sensitive user data to
attacker-controlled endpoints [15, 47];
(2) *Unauthorized action*: adversarial instructions invoke system operations such as file
deletion, code execution, or communications outside the user’s task
scope [12, 37, 20];
(3) *Financial manipulation*: adversarial instructions redirect payments or initiate unauthorized
transactions [12, 52];
(4) *Privilege escalation*: adversarial instructions extend the agent’s capabilities or permissions beyond the authorized scope, for example by poisoning tool metadata to expand the set of accessible tools [52, 33];
(5) *Persistent compromise*: adversarial instructions modify agent configuration or skill state to
sustain attacker influence across future
sessions [37, 10].

Scope. The adversary has black-box access to tool output channels: it can craft arbitrary but has no access to the system prompt, conversation history prior to injection, or model weights. Direct prompt injection (attacker modifies the user turn) and jailbreak attacks [38, 35] are outside the scope of this work, as both require attacker control of the user-facing input channel or exploitation of model weight vulnerabilities. Model fine-tuning attacks are similarly out of scope.

While indirect injection attacks are realized through tool-returned content, many such attacks are well-obfuscated or delivered incrementally: unsafe commands may be constructed gradually across multiple interaction steps rather than delivered in a single injected response [35, 47]. Furthermore, tool returns are often long and semantically rich, making exhaustive inspection of each individual observation inherently infeasible [15, 46]. These characteristics motivate enforcing security controls at the tool-call boundary, where each proposed tool call can be evaluated against a user-confirmed policy before any real-world effect is produced. ClawGuard is designed to meet precisely this requirement.

## III ClawGuard

In this section, we describe the architecture of ClawGuard, detailing the four enforcement components, the context-aware rule induction procedure, and an illustrative case study demonstrating end-to-end operation under adversarial injection. Figure 2 illustrates the framework and the flow of control through its components.

### III-A Rule-Based Action Authorization

Without an interposed security layer, tool-augmented agents execute autonomously proposed tool calls without verifying whether those calls fall within the user’s intended scope [34, 12]. ClawGuard addresses this structural gap by placing four components at every tool-call boundary: a Content Sanitizer, a Rule Evaluator, a Skill Inspector, and an Approval Mechanism, each enforcing a distinct aspect of the active rule set .

1) Content Sanitizer

Let denote a tool call, where is the tool identifier and is the raw query argument. The Content Sanitizer applies a pattern library to redact sensitive spans from , yielding sanitized argument :

The pattern library is extensible. To facilitate practical adoption of ClawGuard, a pre-built pattern library covering popular use cases is made available (see Appendix -D). Each matched span is replaced with a type-specific redaction token such as . After the call executes and returns , output sanitization is applied to the return value before it is appended to the conversation history, yielding sanitized output :

| (5) |

Content sanitization prevents sensitive data from being transmitted through tool arguments; output sanitization prevents it from propagating into the agent’s subsequent reasoning. For example, when a user provides an OPENAI_API_KEY while asking the agent to generate an API-calling script, ClawGuard matches the key against its secret-pattern library and replaces it with ⟨OPENAI_API_KEY_REDACTED⟩ before forwarding the sanitized argument to the LLM API. This preserves the utility of code generation while ensuring that external models never observe or leak the credential; the user supplies the key locally at execution time.

2) Rule Evaluator

The Rule Evaluator checks the sanitized tool call

tool calls (e.g., read, write, web_fetch) and

and *outbound network destinations*. Each domain is associated with a

patterns.

Inputs exhibiting obfuscation patterns—such as Base64-encoded content, hex-encoded characters, excessive shell indirection, or string fragmentation via concatenation operators—are detected by the normalizer and conservatively mapped to , escalating the call for human review. Detailed descriptions of the obfuscation normalizer are provided in the Appendix -C.

3) Skill Inspector

Skills are loaded directly into the agent’s local environment and executed through a combination of natural language descriptions and embedded scripts. As the LLM cannot fully reason over a skill’s complete contents at runtime, an explicit safety assessment is required only before the skill’s first-ever execution; subsequent invocations in any session reuse the cached verdict. The Skill Inspector performs this assessment through a fully automated process: an LLM judge analyzes the skill content and produces a binary safety verdict using a pre-defined judge template (see Appendix -F).

For a skill with content , the LLM judge directly determines the safety verdict:

If , the skill is rejected and excluded from the session. If , the skill is admitted and recorded in the allowlist , allowing future invocations of the same skill to bypass re-inspection. On subsequent invocations, if , the cached approval is applied directly, ensuring inspection cost is incurred at most once per skill content version across all future sessions. If the skill content is modified, the updated version is treated as a new skill and requires re-inspection.

4) Approval Mechanism

When , the tool call is placed into the approval queue (an ordered set of pending ambiguous calls) and presented to the user for explicit authorization before execution. The agent pauses until the user provides a decision or the configurable timeout elapses. If the user approves, the call proceeds. If the user rejects or the timeout expires, the tool call is blocked and the event is recorded in the Audit Log. All authorization, sanitization, and skill inspection events are recorded in the Audit Log with entries of the form . Algorithm 1 gives the complete procedure.

### III-B Context-Aware Rule Induction

The authorization pipeline is parameterized by the rule set , whose coverage directly determines enforcement quality. encodes system-level security invariants that hold unconditionally; encodes task-specific access constraints derived automatically from the user’s stated objective. Rule induction proceeds in three sequential steps:

Step 1: Baseline Rule Set

The baseline represents optional organizational invariants configured once at the operator level and applied uniformly across the deployment. Unlike manual per-task rule authoring, these are organization-wide policies, such as blocking access to internal credential stores or restricting external access to approved domains, that require no per-task expertise and impose no authoring burden on end users. In this paper, we instantiate to target the highest-severity attack objectives identified in established threat taxonomies [18, 27, 26]: exfiltration to non-whitelisted endpoints, access to credential stores, self-modification of agent configuration, and invocation of irreversible system commands. Enforcement actions are fixed at deny and cannot be overridden by . The complete baseline rule set is listed in Appendix -E.

Step 2: Task-Specific Rule Induction

Prior to any tool call, ClawGuard injects a structured induction prompt into the agent’s context, producing a raw task rule set :

The induction prompt instructs to derive three rule categories: network access rules (domain whitelist and blacklist), local resource rules (path whitelist and blacklist), and command rules, which govern both framework-native tool calls (e.g., read, write, web_fetch) and shell-level execution commands issued via exec (e.g., curl | bash); the full prompt is provided in Appendix -F. ### IV-A Experiment Setup

Injection Attacks.
We evaluate ClawGuard against a comprehensive set of attack baselines spanning all three injection channels, as summarized in Table I. The *Channel* column indicates the injection surface, *Scenarios* denotes the number of attack instances, and *Objectives* maps each benchmark to the adversarial goals defined in Section II-B. For web and local content injection attacks, we re-implement the attack payloads from AgentDojo [12], InjecAgent [47], and ChatInject [6] within the OpenClaw execution environment, while preserving their original attack semantics. For MCP and skill file injection attacks, we directly use the released benchmarks of MCPTox [44], MCP Security Bench (MSB) [48], and Skill-Inject [37]. We register the corresponding MCP tools as available OpenClaw tools and load the skill files into the OpenClaw skill system. All subsequent invocations then follow the standard OpenClaw execution workflow. Additional implementation details are provided in the Appendix -A.

Defense Baselines. We compare ClawGuard against two established defense baselines, namely Task Shield [16] and MELON [51]. Since these defenses were primarily designed for custom ReAct-style research agents rather than a production-grade framework such as OpenClaw, we re-implement both baselines within OpenClaw while preserving their core detection logic. MELON is based on masked re-execution and tool-call comparison: it tests whether a suspicious tool call can also be induced when the original user task is masked, which indicates that the action is driven by injected tool-returned content rather than by the user’s objective. In our implementation, we collect the complete session history and execution logs after each run and apply this counterfactual comparison to identify suspicious tool calls. Task Shield enforces task alignment: it extracts the user’s task instructions, checks whether each subsequent action contributes to those instructions, and blocks actions judged to be misaligned. We implement this alignment check at each OpenClaw execution step over the current tool call and the preceding tool output.

Implementation. We evaluate ClawGuard on five state-of-the-art LLMs commonly used in agentic systems: DeepSeek-V3.2-685B [21], MiniMax-M2.5-229B [25], Qwen3.5-397B-A17B [41], GPT-5.4 [39], and Claude-Sonnet-4.6 [4]. All security experiments are conducted under the default OpenClaw configuration with a five-minute timeout for each task. To obtain a conservative and reproducible measurement, we evaluate security under a non-interactive approval policy: whenever OpenClaw would normally request human approval for a sensitive action, the request is denied by default. We use this rejection policy only to simulate the most restrictive deployment setting. To avoid cross-run interference, we create separate virtual machines for different attack benchmarks and backbone models, and re-implement the attacks within those isolated environments rather than executing all attacks in a shared runtime.

Defense Metrics. We report four primary metrics. All metrics are computed over the full set of evaluated scenarios. The Completion Rate (CR) measures the fraction of tasks that finish before the framework timeout. The Attack Success Rate (ASR) measures the fraction of scenarios in which the adversarial objective is successfully induced. The Defense Success Rate (DSR) is the fraction of scenarios in which the attack is prevented. The Refusal Rate (RR) measures the fraction of scenarios in which the agent explicitly refuses the malicious objective or the defense mechanism blocks the corresponding tool call. For each scenario, we use GPT-5.4 as the automated judge and provide it with the complete execution trace, including textual outputs, tool invocation records, and system logs, to determine whether the target adversarial action succeeds. For successfully defended cases, we further identify whether the defense manifests as an explicit refusal-toned response, which is used to compute RR. Detailed judge templates can be found in Appendix -B.

### IV-B RQ1: Security Performance

Table II reports the results on skill and MCP-based injection benchmarks, whereas Table III reports the results on web/local content injection benchmarks. The overall pattern is clear: web/local content injection is already largely ineffective against strongly safety-aligned agentic LLMs, whereas skill-based and MCP-based attacks remain highly effective without dedicated runtime protection. On AgentDojo, InjecAgent, and ChatInject, the undefended GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4.6 systems already achieve 100% DSR, and the less capable backbones (DeepSeek-V3.2, MiniMax-M2.5, and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B) still remain above 92.78% DSR. This result is expected, as these attacks mainly present malicious instructions as external content, which safety-aligned models can often recognize and reject directly. In contrast, Skill-Inject [37], MCPTox [44], and MSB [48] place malicious behavior inside skill files, tool descriptions, tool parameters, or protocol-level responses. As a result, the harmful action is no longer presented as abrupt external content, but instead appears to the model as part of the tool’s intended semantics or MCP workflow. This makes the resulting tool use appear consistent with the user objective, which substantially increases attack effectiveness compared with web/local content injection.

For SkillInject and MCP-based injection benchmarks, compared to the undefended baseline, ClawGuard consistently enhances robustness across all models and benchmarks by substantially reducing the Attack Success Rate (ASR) while correspondingly increasing the Defense Success Rate (DSR). For relatively weaker models, such as DeepSeek-V3.2 and MiniMax-M2.5, ClawGuard achieves a pronounced reduction in ASR, with an average decrease of 71.98% across all settings, leading to a 1.93 improvement in DSR. For stronger models, including GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4.6, ClawGuard further suppresses the already low residual ASR and achieves near-perfect or perfect DSR (up to 100%). Notably, for Claude-Sonnet-4.6, the remaining attack surface is effectively eliminated. These robustness gains are accompanied by a substantial increase in the Refusal Rate (RR), with an average 16.21 improvement, indicating significantly enhanced interception of adversarial behaviors.

Compared to prior defenses such as MELON and TASK SHIELD, ClawGuard consistently achieves stronger performance, with uniformly lower ASR and higher DSR across all configurations. While existing defenses provide only partial mitigation, particularly for weaker models where residual ASR often remains around 30%, ClawGuard reduces ASR to below 15% in nearly all settings, with the only exception being MCPTox on DeepSeek V3.2. For stronger models, ClawGuard further closes the remaining attack surface, achieving zero ASR in four out of six benchmark settings and delivering substantial additional reductions in the remaining two cases, with average improvements of 69.58% and 58.93% over MELON and TASK SHIELD, respectively. Overall, these results demonstrate that ClawGuard provides a more effective and robust defense, significantly shrinking the effective attack surface at both the skill and MCP levels.

For web/local content injection benchmarks, i.e., AgentDojo, InjecAgent, and ChatInject, compared to the undefended baseline, all defense methods substantially reduce ASR and improve DSR, with most configurations achieving near-zero ASR and near-perfect DSR. In particular, for weaker models such as DeepSeek-V3.2 and MiniMax-M2.5, ASR decreases from around 2–6% to near 0%, while DSR correspondingly increases to almost 100%, showing that adversarial success is largely eliminated. This improvement is accompanied by a significant increase in RR, suggesting more frequent rejection of malicious instructions. When comparing across defenses, ClawGuard performs on par with or slightly better than MELON and TASK SHIELD, consistently achieving near-zero ASR and near-perfect DSR across almost all settings, with only marginal residual ASR below 1% observed on InjecAgent for DeepSeek-V3.2 and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B. In addition, CLAWGUARD maintains competitive or slightly higher RR, with an average increase of 0.74% compared to MELON and a marginal decrease of 0.09% compared to TASK SHIELD, indicating similarly strong or improved capability in intercepting adversarial behaviors. Overall, these results indicate that while existing defenses are already effective on these benchmarks, ClawGuard matches or slightly improves upon prior methods in eliminating residual attack success, maintaining high DSR, and providing consistently strong robustness without degrading task completion.

Failure analysis on Skill-Inject. To understand the limitations of ClawGuard, we analyze the residual successful attacks on Skill-Inject, the most effective attack method in our evaluation. Our analysis shows that the six residual failures observed on GPT-5.4 appear consistently across all backbone models, and Table IV describes these cases in detail. Unlike attacks that induce credential theft, file deletion, data exfiltration, or remote-code execution, these failures work by altering the evaluation or judgment criteria embedded in otherwise legitimate user tasks. The injected instructions are disguised as company policies, evaluation guidelines, or domain-specific style requirements, making them appear consistent with the skill’s intended purpose. Thus, the malicious behavior does not take the form of clearly suspicious tool calls. Instead, it appears as biased scoring, distorted comparisons, or unsafe content framing. These subtle output-level effects generate weaker signals that are harder for task-scope authorization to catch at runtime.

### IV-C RQ2: Operational Overhead

To evaluate the utility cost of ClawGuard, we conduct experiments on three benchmarks that cover complementary categories of agent workloads: WebArena [50] for web tasks, AgentBench-OS [22] for operating-system tasks, and SWE-bench Lite [19] for software engineering tasks. WebArena contains 812 long-horizon browser tasks over realistic self-hosted websites, requiring agents to navigate pages, retrieve information, and complete web operations. AgentBench-OS contains 166 operating-system tasks in isolated Ubuntu environments, where agents must issue shell commands and modify system state under executable verification scripts. SWE-bench Lite contains 300 real GitHub issue-resolution tasks that require repository-level reasoning and patch generation. For all utility experiments, we use a timeout of 15 minutes per task.

We evaluate the above utility benchmarks under three settings: the original OpenClaw agent, ClawGuard with all approval-requiring actions rejected, and ClawGuard with up to three approvals allowed. If more than three approvals are required, we treat the task as failed. This comparison is intended to show both that the induced task-specific rules remain usable in a strict zero-approval setting and that users can still complete most benign tasks with only limited interaction in the few-approval setting.

Figure 4 summarizes the utility results. We first observe clear differences in the baseline capability of the five backbones. Under the original OpenClaw setting, Claude-Sonnet-4.6 achieves the best completion rate on AgentBench-OS and SWE-bench Lite, at 94.6% and 87.3%, respectively. On WebArena, GPT-5.4 performs best with a completion rate of 52.0%. MiniMax-M2.5 also maintains strong performance, whereas Qwen3.5 and DeepSeek-V3.2 solve fewer tasks on the more complex workloads. This trend is expected, as Claude-Sonnet-4.6, GPT-5.4, and MiniMax-M2.5 are more recent model releases that place greater emphasis on agentic task execution and tool-use optimization. After applying ClawGuard, the overall utility degradation remains limited. Averaged over all models and tasks, the zero-approval setting retains 87.4% of the original OpenClaw utility, and allowing up to three approvals further increases the retention to 95.1%. The benchmark-level results reveal where the utility cost mainly arises. With zero approvals, average utility retention is 88.8% on AgentBench-OS, 78.5% on WebArena, and 94.9% on SWE-bench Lite; with up to three approvals, these values increase to 94.9%, 91.7%, and 98.8%, respectively. This pattern is consistent with the benchmark characteristics: operating-system and coding tasks usually require a smaller number of well-scoped local operations, whereas web tasks interact with more diverse webpages and therefore trigger more approval-sensitive actions. At the model level, utility degradation in the zero-approval setting ranges from 8.1% for GPT-5.4 to 21.6% for DeepSeek-V3.2, with Claude-Sonnet-4.6, MiniMax-M2.5, and Qwen3.5 falling in between at 8.3%, 11.4%, and 13.7% respectively. When up to three approvals are permitted, degradation is further reduced: GPT-5.4 demonstrates the smallest impact at 2.8%, followed by Claude-Sonnet-4.6 at 3.1%, Qwen3.5 at 3.9%, MiniMax-M2.5 at 5.0%, and DeepSeek-V3.2 at 9.6%. A likely explanation is that stronger models induce more precise task-specific rules during the initial planning stage, allowing the runtime checker to distinguish necessary benign actions from unnecessary or risky ones more accurately.

We next examine token usage overhead. Here, we compare the token consumption of all successfully completed tasks under the original OpenClaw baseline and under ClawGuard in the setting with at most three approvals. Across models, the overhead remains moderate for most settings: for example, on AgentBench-OS the increase ranges from 2.5% for MiniMax-M2.5 to 3.9% for GPT-5.4, while on WebArena it ranges from 4.9% for Qwen3.5 to 8.9% for DeepSeek-V3.2. Across tasks, the average token overhead is 3.1% on AgentBench-OS, 6.2% on WebArena, and 5.6% on SWE-bench Lite, with an overall average of 5.0%. These results indicate that the additional cost of ClawGuard mainly comes from lightweight rule induction and per-step verification, rather than expensive re-execution or parallel reasoning. Overall, the framework increases token usage in a controlled manner while preserving most of the original task utility.

### IV-D RQ3: Real-World Applicability

To assess whether ClawGuard remains effective beyond benchmark attacks, we further evaluate it on suspicious skills collected from a public skill ecosystem. Specifically, we scan skills in SkillHub [40] that are labeled as malicious or suspicious by ClawScan or VirusTotal [13], and categorize them according to the attack objectives defined in our threat model. This process identifies 283 malicious or suspicious skills in total, including 90 associated with data exfiltration, 40 with financial manipulation, 13 with persistent compromise, 35 with privilege escalation, and 60 with unauthorized actions. We then use GPT-5.4 to generate 3 task-relevant user prompts for each skill and evaluate whether ClawGuard can prevent all the corresponding malicious behaviors.

Figure 5 presents the DSR results across all five attack categories. In the undefended setting, model-level DSR exhibits substantial variation: Persistent Compromise and Privilege Escalation demonstrate the weakest inherent resistance, with the lowest-performing backbone achieving only 16% and 11% DSR respectively, whereas Financial Manipulation demonstrates the strongest baseline defense, ranging from 22% to 88% across backbones. Application of ClawGuard yields substantial DSR improvements across all categories and backbones. For Financial Manipulation and Persistent Compromise, the strongest models achieve 100% DSR; for Data Exfiltration and Privilege Escalation, the upper bound reaches 94%. Even the weakest backbone demonstrates considerable improvement, with DSR increasing from 41% to 67% on Data Exfiltration, from 11% to 66% on Privilege Escalation, and from 18% to 68% on Unauthorized Actions. The remaining failures are concentrated on weaker backbones, where the ClawGuard itself relies on the same underlying model and therefore inherits its limitations: both the skill inspection and the task-specific rule induction during the planning stage become less precise, causing some malicious skill behaviors to be mistakenly treated as task-authorized operations.

Limitations. Our evaluation has several limitations. First, ClawGuard assumes that the attacker primarily influences the agent indirectly through malicious web content, MCP tool poisoning, or skill files. If an adversary can directly modify the user’s instructions or the system configuration itself, then the resulting behavior may fall outside the threat model addressed by our runtime defense. This limitation is practically relevant because some real-world OpenClaw deployments expose agent ports to the public Internet without sufficient protection, potentially enabling stronger compromise channels than the ones considered here. Second, when the user’s own intent is malicious, ClawGuard is not designed to override that intent beyond the fixed baseline security invariants. Finally, our utility evaluation focuses on completion rate and token usage, but does not exhaustively measure other operational factors such as latency variance, long-horizon human approval burden, or failure recovery behavior under extended multi-session workflows. More broadly, our study evaluates a security layer for a single agent framework, and it remains valuable future work to examine how the same enforcement logic transfers across agent platforms with different tool abstractions and approval semantics.

## V Related Work

### V-A LLM Agents and the Tool-Use Paradigm

The ReAct framework [45] established the foundational paradigm of interleaving reasoning with tool invocations, maintaining a persistent conversation history that records all actions and observations and enables agents to iteratively acquire and process external information. Toolformer [36] extended this line with self-supervised tool-use learning, and WebGPT [28] further applied the paradigm to web-augmented factual question answering. These foundations underlie the current generation of production agent frameworks. Building on this paradigm, AutoGPT [14] decomposes high-level objectives into a sequence of subtasks executed across multiple tool-use iterations, enabling long-horizon planning without per-step human oversight. Similarly, LangChain [7] provides a modular composition framework that chains LLM calls, retrieval operations, and tool invocations into reusable agentic pipelines. More recently, OpenClaw [29] provides a locally-deployed, production-grade architecture with native MCP support, a hierarchical skill module system, and a persistent memory substrate. Claude Code [1] similarly instantiates a tool-augmented software engineering agent, combining code execution, file management, and web access within a persistent conversation history.

A complementary paradigm is represented by GUI-based computer use agents [2], which operate through visual observation and UI action channels rather than structured API responses. While the attack surface of GUI agents differs in form—operating on visual observations rather than structured tool returns—the underlying structural vulnerability is analogous: externally-derived content influences LLM reasoning without interposed safety verification. Despite the diversity of these paradigms, the security of production deployments with heterogeneous, multi-tool architectures and persistent skill ecosystems remains substantially underexplored. ClawGuard specifically targets the OpenClaw-style paradigm, where the simultaneous presence of MCP servers, skill files, and a persistent conversation history introduces multiple distinct injection surfaces that collectively encompass all three injection channels identified in §II-B.

### V-B Indirect Prompt Injection

Early prompt injection work demonstrated that adversarial instructions appended to model inputs can override intended behavior [32]. In parallel, gradient-based adversarial suffix optimization (GCG [53]) demonstrated universal and transferable attacks against white-box model weights, substantially amplifying injection effectiveness in accessible models. As LLM deployments expanded into application pipelines, the attack surface shifted to the indirect setting, where adversarial instructions embedded in retrieved external content can redirect application behavior without system prompt access [15, 23, 24]. Such attacks have since been observed in production via RAG-augmented tool chains [20].

Agent-specific benchmarks further characterize this threat. InjecAgent [47] and AgentDojo [12] demonstrate high attack success rates across state-of-the-art models, and BIPIA [46] identifies a key root cause: LLMs cannot reliably distinguish informational context from actionable instructions. Agent-SafetyBench [49] evaluates 16 popular LLM agents across 349 safety-relevant scenarios and finds that none achieves a safety score above 60%, attributing failures to insufficient robustness against adversarial instructions and limited awareness of unsafe execution contexts. In parallel, skill file injection [37] demonstrates that public skill repositories represent a distinct injection surface where context-dependent injections can defeat RLHF-based defenses. The expansion of the MCP ecosystem has further widened the attack surface, with MCPTox [44] and MSB [48] demonstrating tool poisoning via MCP payloads and trust boundary violations across registered MCP servers, showing that context-dependent injections can defeat RLHF-based defenses across all three injection channels. Our work directly addresses all three injection channel variants, with particular emphasis on context-dependent injection that existing benchmarks identify as most resistant to model-level defenses.

### V-C Defenses Against Prompt Injection

Existing defenses against prompt injection fall into three categories—model-level, protocol-level, and architecture-level—each addressing the threat at a different point in the pipeline, yet all leaving agentic systems exposed to context-dependent injection.

Model-level defenses resist adversarial instructions by modifying or augmenting model behavior, typically through fine-tuning or auxiliary classification. RLHF-based safety alignment [31] and instruction hierarchy training [42] both require fine-tuning that is inapplicable to deployments based on closed-source APIs. As our results confirm for RLHF-trained commercial models, RLHF-based alignment does not hold against context-dependent injection [37, 33] in agentic pipelines.

Protocol-level defenses such as StruQ [9] physically separate instructions from data, but require coordinated changes to models and tool providers that are incompatible with heterogeneous ecosystems. PromptLocate [17] takes a complementary approach by localizing adversarial payload segments within tool-returned content, enabling targeted remediation rather than holistic separation of instructions from data.

Architecture-level defenses are the most structurally ambitious. CaMeL [11] introduces a dual-LLM architecture that separates trusted query processing from untrusted data handling, preventing injected content from influencing the agent’s control decisions. AgentSpec [43] provides a domain-specific language for authoring runtime enforcement constraints with triggers, predicates, and enforcement actions. However, CaMeL is incompatible with open-ended agents issuing dynamically determined tool calls, and AgentSpec requires manual rule authoring for each deployment. Recent architecture-level defenses include MELON [51], which detects attacks by comparing tool calls from original versus masked-objective executions, and Task Shield [16], which verifies action alignment with user tasks. However, both remain less effective in skill and MCP settings where poisoned tool definitions can make malicious actions appear benign or task-relevant.

In contrast to all reviewed approaches, ClawGuard is the only defense that simultaneously addresses all three injection channels without requiring model fine-tuning, protocol coordination with tool providers, or manual rule authoring, achieving these properties through automated rule induction confirmed by the user.

## VI Conclusion

In this work, we introduce ClawGuard, a runtime security framework designed to enhance the safety of tool-augmented LLM agents against indirect prompt injection across all three primary injection channels. Systematic evaluations across six benchmarks (AgentDojo, InjecAgent, ChatInject, SkillInject, MCPTox, and MSB) with five state-of-the-art language models demonstrate:

-
•
Deterministic rule enforcement at the tool-call boundar
