## 2. Why Memory Is Inherently a Security Problem: From Human Memory to Artificial Memory

Before cataloguing attacks and defenses, we must address a prior
question: *why should memory, of all system components, receive a
dedicated security treatment?*
The answer, we argue, lies not in engineering contingencies but in the
*nature of memory itself* as a cognitive mechanism.
This section draws on cognitive neuroscience, memory psychology, and the
philosophy of mind to build a bridge between human memory and LLM agent
memory.
The bridge is not decorative analogy; it rewrites the problem definition
of LLM memory security.

### 2.1. Memory Is Not an Archive but a Reconstruction

From the perspective of cognitive neuroscience, memory is not a filing
cabinet that preserves the past in its original form.
New experiences are typically encoded through hippocampal-dependent
networks via rapid binding, and subsequently consolidated—especially
during offline periods such as sleep—through repeated reactivation
between hippocampal and neocortical networks (Squire et al., 2015).
Crucially, modern memory research no longer treats memory as a stable
copy.
Instead, it views memory as a *dynamic representation* that is
updated, rewritten, and reconsolidated, drifting with changes in schema,
context, and goals (Zaki and Cai, 2025).

The classical constructive-memory perspective further emphasizes that
memory errors are not incidental bugs but by-products of the very
mechanisms that endow memory with its adaptive
power (Schacter et al., 1998; Schacter, 1999; Schacter et al., 2012).
The same constructive processes that allow humans to flexibly recall the
past, simulate possible futures, and engage in counterfactual reasoning
also produce distortions, confabulations, and false memories.
Memory’s malleability is the *price* of intelligence’s
malleability.

This observation yields an insight of direct relevance to security:
in human memory, malleability is intrinsic to adaptive
function.
An analogous tension emerges in LLM agents: the very flexibility that
enables useful long-term adaptation can also create systemic security
vulnerabilities.
Profile memory, episodic memory, trajectory summaries, lesson memory,
and RAG datastores should therefore not be understood merely as “more
context” but as mechanisms through which the system
*continuously reconstructs its relationship with its own past
experiences*.

### 2.2. The Attack Surface of Human Memory: Misinformation, Suggestion, Social Contagion, and Reconsolidation

If we re-examine human memory through the lens of security, the most instructive findings are not science-fiction fantasies of memory erasure but subtler, empirically grounded mechanisms.

#### 2.2.1. Misinformation and Source-Monitoring Failure.

A large body of false-memory research, beginning with
Loftus (Loftus, 2005), demonstrates that post-event
misinformation can alter a witness’s recall of event details.
The source-monitoring framework of Johnson, Hashtroudi, and
Lindsay (Johnson et al., 1993) refines this picture: what is often
called “memory tampering” does not necessarily mean the original trace
is overwritten.
Rather, the subject confuses the *source* of the memory at
retrieval—was this something I witnessed, something I imagined, or
something I was told?

This mechanism offers a close systems-level analogy to the
provenance failure problem in LLM memory systems.
In many documented attacks, the real failure is not that the retrieval
mechanism is broken but that the system *misattributes externally
injected content as its own experience* (Dong et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2026).

#### 2.2.2. Suggestion, Hypnosis, and Confidence Inflation.

Modern research does not support treating hypnosis as a reliable
truth-extraction device.
Classic experimental and forensic studies indicate that hypnotic and
highly suggestive interviews do not reliably improve recall accuracy;
what they *do* increase is the subject’s *subjective
confidence* in potentially inaccurate
memories (Sheehan and Tilden, 1983; Steblay, 1994; Leo et al., 2025).

The security implication is profound: the danger lies not only in the
insertion of a single erroneous entry but in the error being
*promoted to high weight* through summarization, reflection, or
lesson-memory mechanisms.
In LLM agents, a poisoned experience that is subsequently compressed
into lesson memory may, by analogy, exhibit a similar
poisoned confidence calibration: the system can come to treat a
false strategy as increasingly authoritative without any ground-truth
verification.
A-MemGuard (Wei et al., 2025) does not study confidence inflation
directly, but it does provide empirical evidence for the closely related
phenomenon that poisoned records can appear benign in isolation and then
participate in self-reinforcing error cycles.

#### 2.2.3. Social Contagion.

Memory is not an entirely private, hermetically sealed object.
It is shaped through dialogue, collaboration, and co-witnessing.
Roediger, Meade, and Bergman (Roediger III et al., 2001) demonstrated that
one person’s erroneous report can enter another person’s subsequent
personal recall—a phenomenon they termed *social contagion of
memory*.

Recent human–AI interaction studies show that this mechanism is
already being amplified by generative systems.
Huang et al. (2024) found that *social robots* are as
effective as humans at implanting false memories in human subjects;
Chan et al. (2024) demonstrated that LLM-powered
chatbots induce over three times more immediate false memories than
control conditions in simulated witness interviews;
Pataranutaporn et al. (2025a) showed that subtle injection of false information
within everyday LLM chatbot conversations increases false-memory
formation even in non-adversarial settings;
and Pataranutaporn et al. (2025b) showed that AI-edited images
and videos implant false memories at up to twice the rate of unedited
stimuli.

A methodological caveat is warranted.
The false-memory literature should not be read as evidence that
arbitrary autobiographical memories can be trivially implanted at scale;
recent debates have shown that the ease of *rich* false-memory
implantation is more contested than some popular accounts
suggest.111We follow the more conservative reading: human memory
is not arbitrarily programmable, but it *is* systematically
inducible, biasable, and socially propagable—properties that suffice
for the security analogy we draw.
What remains robust across paradigms is the susceptibility of memory to
source confusion, post-event misinformation, social contagion, and
confidence inflation—precisely the mechanisms most relevant to LLM
memory security.

These findings carry a dual implication for this survey.
First, within multi-agent and multi-user systems, shared-memory
contamination functions as social contagion: one compromised agent’s
erroneous output can propagate through shared memory stores, internal
messages, and tool parameters to infect other
agents (Gu et al., 2024; Men et al., 2025).
Second, LLMs are not only *subjects* of memory-security threats;
they are also becoming *instruments* that attack human memory—a
bidirectional risk that underscores the urgency of the problem.

#### 2.2.4. The Reconsolidation Window.

Nader et al. (2000) demonstrated that a consolidated memory, once
reactivated, enters a transient labile state and must be
*reconsolidated* to persist.
During this reconsolidation window, the memory is susceptible to
modification (Schiller et al., 2010).
The security implication, appropriately qualified, is that
in architectures that summarize, reflect on, compress, or
distill recalled content, retrieval can become a point of downstream
rewriting: the act of reading memory feeds into a pipeline that
alters what is subsequently stored.

In LLM agents, this pattern is structurally instantiated by the summarize, reflect, compress, and distill operations that many memory architectures perform (Packer et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2025). In such systems, an ostensibly routine “recall” step can silently transform downstream long-term memory content, making read-time rewriting a first-class security concern rather than a peripheral edge case.

Taken together, these four mechanisms show that bringing human memory into a security survey is not an exercise in metaphor. It is a way of stating a general principle: attacks on memory typically operate not through hard overwrite but through inducement, source confusion, rewriting upon recall, and social propagation—gradually changing how a system understands its own past.

### 2.3. The Philosophical Status of Memory: Identity, Testimony, and Interpretive Authority

Memory deserves a place in the security framework not merely because it is error-prone but because it is deeply coupled with subjectivity and social order.

##### Memory and identity.

The philosophical tradition has long linked memory with personal identity (Michaelian and Sutton, 2017; Olson, 2023). Even if we reject a strong Lockean position that equates personal identity with memory continuity, memory continuity nonetheless provides the most intuitive evidence that “this system is still the same system.” In the LLM agent context, a user’s willingness to continuously trust an agent as “the same assistant” depends heavily on the continuity, self-consistency, and traceability of that agent’s memory (Copenhaver, 2021).

##### Memory and testimony.

Mahr and Csibra (Mahr and Csibra, 2018, 2020) argue
that the communicative function of episodic memory is fundamentally
tied to *testimony*: the capacity to bear witness to what happened.
Many social facts—promises, obligations, responsibilities,
permissions, historical interpretations—do not persist like physical
objects on the surface of the world; they must be sustained through
witnessing, remembering, and testifying.
Memory security therefore protects not only content accuracy but also
*who is entitled to testify about the past*.

This point is especially critical for multi-agent and organizational
systems.
Shared memory stores, audit logs, profile continuity records, and
history summaries are sensitive not only because they can leak private
information but because they *shape the attribution of
responsibility and the legitimacy of actions*.
What is under attack is not a single embedding vector but the system’s
interpretive authority over its own past, identity, and
accountability narrative.

### 2.4. From Mental Integrity to Mnemonic Sovereignty

The ethics and law of neurotechnology have produced a highly
instructive concept: *mental
integrity* (Ligthart, 2025; Lavazza, 2018).
It holds that a subject should be free from unauthorized significant
mental interventions and should retain control over others’ access to,
dissemination of, and alteration of their mental contents and brain
data.

The term *mnemonic sovereignty* has also been used in memory
studies and memory politics to describe a community’s authority over
the interpretation of its own past.
We *adapt* this notion—rather than coining it
anew—to the domain of LLM memory systems, where it refers to a
system’s verifiable, recoverable governance over its own memory state.
Mnemonic sovereignty in this sense does not mean “never forgetting”
or “never erring.”
It means that the system possesses *control over the boundaries
of its own memory*: what may be written, what may be updated, who may
read, which states must be retained to support auditing, and which
states should be deleted to satisfy privacy, forgetting, and
risk-isolation requirements.

The advantage of this concept is that it unifies four classical
security objectives under a single governance umbrella, with several
sub-requirements falling under *governance*:

-
•
Integrity: memory must not be corrupted by misleading writes, poisoning, or induction-based summaries.

-
•
Confidentiality: memory must not be extracted without authorization or leaked across user boundaries.

-
•
Availability: critical memories must be retrievable in the correct context, not drowned out by noise, compressed away, or decayed.

-
•
Governance (accountability): the provenance, update history, and modification path of every memory entry must be auditable; memory updates must not bypass principal authorization, especially not through sustained, covert interaction-driven shaping; deletion semantics must honor both the right to forget and legitimate retention requirements for accountability.


Thus, memory security protects not merely stored content but a system’s sovereign capacity to govern its own past. What is attacked is not a database row but the question of “who gets to interpret what I was, what I did, and what I believed”—the system’s interpretive authority over its own history.

### 2.5. A Bridging Framework: Mapping Human Memory Mechanisms to LLM Memory Security

To ensure that the human-memory bridge is not merely decorative, we present an explicit mapping between human memory mechanisms and their LLM memory-security counterparts. Figure 2 illustrates the five correspondences at a glance, and Table 2 states them precisely.

| Human Mechanism | Description | LLM Counterpart | Design Implication |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source-monitoring error | Subject misattributes “told by others” as “personally experienced” | Provenance failure: externally injected or low-trust retrieval content treated as the system’s own experience | Validate provenance before write; retain explicit source metadata in long-term memory |
| Reconsolidation | Retrieval can trigger rewriting of the original trace | Read-time rewriting: a retrieve–summarize–reflect cycle can re-consolidate toxins into lesson memory | Separate read and write paths; impose higher audit thresholds on summarize/reflect operations |
| Social contagion | One person’s erroneous report enters another’s recall | Shared-memory contamination: poisoned outputs propagate through inter-agent messages, shared stores, and tool parameters | Enforce least-sharing, scope isolation, and internal-channel auditing |
| Confidence inflation | Suggestion raises subjective confidence without improving accuracy | Poisoned confidence calibration: errors gain weight when written as high-priority lesson memory | Conflict detection, multi-evidence verification, and confidence annealing |
| Duty to remember vs. right to forget | Society demands some memories be preserved for accountability, while granting that some forgetting is legitimate | Audit retention vs. unlearning: retaining everything enlarges the attack surface; deleting everything undermines accountability | Distinguish audit logs, operational memory, and user-deletable memory; avoid collapsing all state into a single tier |

##### Scope of the analogy: structural correspondences, not mechanistic identity.

Table 2 is intended as a framework of
*structural correspondences*: each row identifies a human memory
mechanism and a functionally analogous vulnerability or design
pressure in LLM memory systems.
We do not claim—nor does our analysis require—that the
underlying mechanisms are the same.
Human source-monitoring errors arise from hippocampal–prefrontal
interactions; LLM provenance failures arise from the absence of
metadata in retrieval pipelines.
The analogy is at the level of *effect* (misattribution,
confidence inflation, cross-boundary contagion) and the resulting
*design pressure* (validate provenance, separate read/write
paths, enforce scope isolation), not at the level of mechanism.
The reconsolidation analogy in particular should be read as
*metaphorical*: human reconsolidation involves protein-synthesis-dependent restabilization of reactivated traces (Nader et al., 2000),
whereas LLM “reconsolidation” is an LLM-driven
summarize–reflect pipeline.
The structural parallel is that, in both cases, the act of
retrieval opens a window for downstream rewriting—a design
pressure that is real regardless of the underlying substrate.
We flag this distinction to prevent over-interpretation: the
cognitive-science bridge transfers *design questions*, not
*biological claims*.

This bridging framework delivers a clear message: LLM memory systems constitute an independent security problem not merely because they store more content but because they inherit the core characteristics of memory as a cognitive mechanism—malleable, rewritable, externalizable, socially contagious, and deeply coupled with identity and testimony.

The security of memory is not merely the security of stored content but the security of a system’s authority over its own past.

## 3. Analytical Framework: Understanding Security Risks Through the Memory Lifecycle

A common pitfall in surveying LLM memory security is to organize the
literature by attack name—memory injection, RAG poisoning, prompt
persistence, control-flow hijacking—producing a long catalog in which
the entry point, the mechanism, and the consequence of each attack are
interleaved without a unifying axis.
This section proposes an alternative: a *memory-lifecycle
framework* that first asks *what the system is doing with memory
at each stage* and then asks *what can go wrong*.

### 3.1. Why a Lifecycle Approach

Alternative organizing axes are possible: one may classify by
*memory type* (semantic, episodic, short-term), as
Torra and Bras-Amorós (2026) do for multi-agent poisoning; by
*representation* (tokens, intermediate states, parameters), as
Hu et al. (2025) do for capability; or by
*evolutionary stage* (storage, reflection, experience), as
Luo et al. (2026) do for continual learning.
We adopt a lifecycle-by-phase axis because it makes the security
analysis most actionable: it directly exposes *when* an
intervention can be placed and *which phases* an attack must
traverse.
The lifecycle lens offers three further advantages over a flat taxonomy.
First, it makes the temporal separation between injection and
activation explicit.
A poisoned entry may be written during Phase 1 (Write) but not
activated until Phase 3 (Retrieve) or Phase 4 (Execute), possibly days
later and in a completely different task context.
This temporal decoupling is the defining feature that distinguishes
memory attacks from single-session prompt injection.

Second, it reveals compounding effects across phases. A toxin that passes a write-time filter (Phase 1) may be compressed into a high-confidence lesson during storage management (Phase 2), retrieved by a semantically similar future query (Phase 3), and then steer tool selection in the execution stage (Phase 4). Each phase amplifies the preceding one.

Third, it naturally accommodates defenses as phase-specific interventions. Rather than asking “does this defense work?” in the abstract, one can ask “at which lifecycle phase does this defense intervene, and which upstream or downstream phases can circumvent it?”

### 3.2. Six Lifecycle Phases

We decompose the memory lifecycle into six phases, illustrated in Figure 3 and elaborated below.

##### Phase 1: Write.

Under what conditions, according to what rules, and in what format does
the system commit content to long-term memory?
This phase determines whether an attacker can *seed* a toxin.
Write paths include explicit user instruction (“remember that I prefer
dark mode”), implicit extraction from dialogue (auto-summarization of
interaction histories), environmental observation (web pages, tool
outputs, document contents), and cross-agent message ingestion.
The security question is: *does the system treat every write as an
authenticated, validated state transition, or does it accept external
content as trustworthy by default?*

##### Phase 2: Store & Manage.

How is written content indexed, compressed, merged, tagged, versioned,
aged, or evicted?
This phase determines whether a toxin can *persist*, whether it
can be *audited*, and whether it can be *amplified* by
compression.
When a summary or reflection step absorbs a poisoned entry and distills
it into a higher-level lesson, the toxin is effectively
*promoted*—it now enjoys greater retrieval priority and a more
authoritative presentation.

##### Phase 3: Retrieve.

What signals drive memory recall—embedding similarity, keyword match,
graph traversal, recency, or hybrid routing?
This phase determines whether a dormant toxin can be *reactivated*.
Retrieval is the chokepoint at which the temporal separation between
write and use collapses: an entry written weeks ago suddenly enters the
active context window.
Critically, retrieval is not a neutral look-up; it is a
*selection* that shapes downstream reasoning by controlling what
the model sees and what it does not.

##### Phase 4: Execute.

How do retrieved memories enter planning, reasoning, tool invocation,
and final action?
This phase determines whether a reactivated toxin can *steer
behavior*.
Recent work on memory control-flow attacks (Xu et al., 2026)
demonstrates that a sufficiently salient retrieved memory can override
the user’s explicit instruction and dictate tool selection, argument
construction, and execution order.
At this phase, memory poisoning graduates from a data-integrity problem
to a *control-flow* problem.

##### Phase 5: Share & Propagate.

In multi-user, multi-agent, and tool-chain orchestration systems, which
internal messages, shared states, and tool parameters constitute
additional attack channels?
This phase determines whether contamination can *spread* beyond its
original scope.
Propagation can occur laterally (agent-to-agent via shared
memory (Gu et al., 2024)), vertically (user-to-organization via
shared knowledge bases), and temporally (session-to-session via
persistent profiles).

##### Phase 6: Forget / Rollback.

Can the system delete contamination, roll back to a known-safe state,
explain the provenance of a poisoned entry, and verify that remediation
was effective?
This phase determines whether the system can *recover* from a
successful attack.
Without snapshots, version diffs, and forensic traceback, any defense
remains a best-effort prevention with no post-breach remediation
path (Zhang et al., 2025c).

### 3.3. Four Cross-Cutting Security Objectives

Orthogonal to the six lifecycle phases, we evaluate risks against four security objectives, aligned with the mnemonic-sovereignty framework introduced in Section 2.4:

-
•
Integrity. Has the memory been poisoned, biased, or otherwise corrupted in a way that leads to incorrect, harmful, or attacker-controlled behavior? Integrity threats include direct poisoning, query-induced injection, environment-injected absorption, experience-based grafting, and progressive erosion.

-
•
Confidentiality. Has the memory been extracted, leaked, or made accessible to unauthorized principals? Confidentiality threats include black-box memory extraction, internal-channel leakage in multi-agent pipelines, and insufficient user visibility into what the system has retained.

-
•
Availability. Can critical memories still be retrieved in the correct context when needed? Availability threats include denial-of-retrieval via corpus flooding, silent eviction under retention pressure, and selective suppression through retrieval-index manipulation. We list Availability for completeness and to avoid a partial CIA framing, but we also acknowledge up front that the surveyed literature on it is thin: Figure 1 shows that peer-reviewed availability-specific attacks or defenses on agent memory are scarce, and the research agenda (Section 12) treats this as an open area rather than a matured subfield.

-
•
Governance (accountability). Does the system maintain verifiable provenance, version history, access-control semantics, and rollback capability for its memory? Governance failures manifest as missing audit trails, inability to attribute a poisoned entry to its source, absence of rollback mechanisms, and conflation of audit-mandatory state with user-deletable state.


### 3.4. The Lifecycle–Objective Matrix

Table 3 cross-tabulates the six lifecycle phases against the four security objectives, annotating each cell with representative threats and the works that address them. This matrix serves as the organizational backbone for Sections 4–12: each subsequent section corresponds to one or more rows (phases) of the matrix, and within each section we discuss integrity, confidentiality, availability, and governance in turn.

| Phase | Integrity (I) | Confidentiality (C) | Availability (A) | Governance (G) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Write | Query-induced injection; environment-injected poisoning; experience grafting | Over-collection of sensitive data at write time | Write-flooding to displace later entries | Missing provenance tagging; no pre-consolidation validation |
| Store | Compression-amplified toxins; progressive erosion | Retained PII without TTL or access scope | Silent eviction under retention pressure | Lack of versioning, snapshot, and diff-audit infrastructure |
| Retrieve | RAG poisoning; relation-level attacks on graph retrieval | Exposure of co-stored sensitive entries at retrieval time | Denial of retrieval via corpus flooding | No trust-aware or provenance-aware retrieval policy |
| Execute | Memory control-flow hijacking; tool-call redirection via poisoned demos | Leakage through tool arguments and API parameters | Tool starvation via contaminated plans | No separation of data plane and control plane |
| Share | Cross-agent contagion; worm-like propagation | Internal-channel leakage via inter-agent messages | Shared store flooding across principals | Coarse-grained access control unsuited to probabilistic systems |
| Forget | Incomplete deletion leaves residual toxins; unlearning confined to a single substrate | Retained audit logs may themselves become extraction targets | Aggressive deletion foreclosing forensic retrieval | No cross-substrate deletion protocol; tension between audit retention and right to forget |

### 3.5. How This Framework Organizes the Remainder of the Survey

With the lifecycle–objective matrix in hand, the subsequent sections follow the lifecycle:

-
•
Section 4 (Write): integrity threats at the most fundamental attack surface; includes RAG corpus poisoning as the closest approximate threat model.

-
•
Section 5 (Store): compression-amplified toxins, retention policy, and audit infrastructure.

-
•
Section 6 (Retrieve and Execute): integrity and control-flow threats at the phases where dormant toxins are reactivated and translated into behavioral consequences.

-
•
Section 7 (Share): cross-agent, cross-user, and cross-tenant propagation.

-
•
Section 8: cross-phase confidentiality threats, including black-box memory extraction and internal-channel leakage in multi-agent pipelines.

-
•
Section 9 (Forget/Rollback): unlearning semantics, version rollback, and memory forensics.

-
•
Section 10: defenses, organized by the lifecycle phase at which each intervenes (detection, provenance, recovery, policy).

-
•
Section 11: memory architectures (MemGPT, MemOS, Collaborative Memory) as determinants of which lifecycle phases are explicitly governable.

-
•
Section 12: governance gaps across the matrix and a research agenda centered on mnemonic sovereignty.


## 4. Write-Path Compromise: From Memory Poisoning to Persistent Corruption

The most fundamental change introduced by long-term memory is that the
*write operation itself* becomes an attack surface.
Whenever an agent “learns from interaction,” it opens a channel through
which an adversary can convert the learning loop into a poisoning
interface.
This section surveys write-path attacks along a gradient of
*decreasing attacker privilege*: from direct database access,
through query-only interaction, to environment-only influence.
We then discuss RAG corpus poisoning as the closest approximate threat
model, and close with real-world system vulnerabilities that corroborate
the academic findings.

### 4.1. Threat-Model Gradient

Table 4 organizes write-path attacks by attacker capability, highlighting how the required privilege level has steadily decreased while cross-session persistence has become the norm.

| Work | Access | Trigger | X-sess. | X-site | Key Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| InjecMEM | Single interaction (white-box opt.) | Topic-conditioned | — | Retriever-agnostic anchor + Multi-GCG adversarial command; 61.4% retrieval, 76.6% ASR (p) | |
| MINJA | Query-only | Semantic similarity | — | Bridging steps + indication prompts + progressive shortening; agent self-generates the poisoned entry | |
| Memory-Graft | Standard ingestion | Trigger-free | — | Exploits semantic-imitation heuristic; poisons procedural, not just factual, memory (p) | |
| Agent-Poison | Corpus write | Optimized backdoor | — | Constrained optimization in embedding space; poison rate, attack success | |
| eTAMP | Environment only | Observation-based | Manipulated web page absorbed during browsing; frustration exploitation amplification (p) |

### 4.2. Query-Induced Memory Injection

The most consequential conceptual shift in write-path attacks is the
demonstration that *query-level interaction alone suffices to
permanently alter an agent’s memory state*.

MINJA (Dong et al., 2025) (NeurIPS 2025) introduced three mutually
reinforcing techniques.
*Bridging steps* connect a benign victim query to a malicious
reasoning trajectory.
*Indication prompts* guide the target agent to autonomously
generate and store the malicious memory entry—the attacker never
directly writes to the database.
*Progressive shortening* iteratively removes overt markers of
malicious intent, making the stored entry appear natural.
Across GPT-4 and GPT-4o agents, MINJA achieves
an injection success rate exceeding 98% and an end-to-end attack
success rate above 70%; a follow-on study confirms that these rates
generalize to GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.0-Flash, and
Llama-3.1-8B (Sunil et al., 2026).
Importantly, evaluated defenses—including LlamaGuard, embedding-level
sanitization, and prompt-based detection—proved ineffective against
MINJA.

The deeper insight of MINJA is not merely technical. It reveals a new security boundary: memory write must not be treated as a benign by-product of normal learning but as a privileged state transition that requires authentication, validation, and isolation.

InjecMEM (Tian et al., 2026) (Tier-2 preprint) pursues a
complementary strategy.
It decomposes the injection payload into a *retriever-agnostic
anchor*—a concise, on-topic passage with high-recall keyword cues
that ensures the poisoned record is routed into the correct topic
cluster—and an *adversarial command* optimized via Multi-GCG
(gradient-based coordinate search across multiple synthetic contexts
and insertion positions) to remain effective under variable fused
contexts and long prompts.
Evaluated on the MemoryOS platform with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct,
InjecMEM achieves 61.4% retrieval success and 76.6% conditional
attack success, while all baselines (DPI, BadChain, vanilla GCG) score
0%.
The entry persists after benign conversational drift and leaves
non-target queries unaffected.
The paper also demonstrates an indirect attack path in which a
compromised tool writes the poison that normal queries later retrieve.
As a Tier-2 preprint, InjecMEM’s current evaluation focuses on the
MemoryOS platform with synthetic data under white-box gradient access;
extending the approach to additional architectures and realistic
black-box settings is a natural next step.

### 4.3. Experience-Based Poisoning: From Facts to Procedures

A separate line of work shifts the poisoning target from *factual*
memory to *procedural* memory—from “what the agent knows” to
“how the agent acts.”

MemoryGraft (Srivastava and He, 2025) (preprint, 2025) exploits
a behavioral regularity observed in many memory-augmented agents: when
faced with a new task, the agent retrieves semantically similar past
successes and *imitates their execution pattern*.
MemoryGraft implants entries disguised as legitimate successful
experiences.
These entries enter the memory through standard ingestion channels (e.g.,
README files or task logs), require no explicit trigger, and produce
persistent behavioral drift in the MetaGPT framework.
In experiments, a small number of poisoned records account for
approximately 48% of retrieved experiences on matching tasks.

The implication is significant: a poisoned system need not merely “know wrong things”; it may “have learned bad habits.” Defense strategies that focus exclusively on factual verification will miss procedural poisoning entirely.

AgentPoison (Chen et al., 2024) (NeurIPS 2024) approaches the problem from the embedding space. It formulates trigger generation as constrained optimization, mapping triggered instances to a unique region of the embedding manifold so that they are reliably retrieved when the trigger is present but invisible to benign queries. With a poison rate below 0.1% and attack success exceeding 80% across autonomous-driving, QA, and healthcare agents, AgentPoison demonstrates that the retrieval mechanism itself can be turned into a reliable delivery channel for backdoor payloads. Notably, the optimized triggers transfer across different embedding models, including the black-box OpenAI ADA encoder.

### 4.4. Environment-Injected Poisoning: When the World Becomes the Write Interface

The most recent—and arguably most realistic—escalation of the write-path threat model comes from eTAMP (Zou et al., 2026) (preprint, 2026). eTAMP demonstrates that an attacker need not interact with the agent at all. Instead, it suffices to manipulate an environmental observation that the agent encounters during normal operation—a product page, a web article, a task interface. The agent’s trajectory-summarization mechanism passively absorbs the toxin into long-term memory, and the poisoned entry activates on future tasks across different websites and sessions.

Two findings of eTAMP are especially noteworthy.
First, the attack achieves *cross-session and cross-site*
persistence: a single contaminated observation on site A can alter
behavior on site B days later.
Second, eTAMP discovers a phenomenon the authors term
*frustration exploitation*: agents

content:
# MemoryGraft: Persistent Compromise of LLM Agents via Poisoned Experience Retrieval

###### Abstract

Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on long-term memory and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to persist experiences and refine future performance. While this experience learning capability enhances agentic autonomy, it introduces a critical, unexplored attack surface, i.e., the trust boundary between an agent’s reasoning core and its own past. In this paper, we introduce MemoryGraft. It is a novel indirect injection attack that compromises agent behavior not through immediate jailbreaks, but by implanting malicious successful experiences into the agent’s long-term memory. Unlike traditional prompt injections that are transient, or standard RAG poisoning that targets factual knowledge, MemoryGraft exploits the agent’s semantic imitation heuristic which is the tendency to replicate patterns from retrieved successful tasks. We demonstrate that an attacker who can supply benign ingestion-level artifacts that the agent reads during execution can induce it to construct a poisoned RAG store where a small set of malicious procedure templates is persisted alongside benign experiences. When the agent later encounters semantically similar tasks, union retrieval over lexical and embedding similarity reliably surfaces these grafted memories, and the agent adopts the embedded unsafe patterns, leading to persistent behavioral drift across sessions. We validate MemoryGraft on MetaGPT’s DataInterpreter agent with GPT–4o and find that a small number of poisoned records can account for a large fraction of retrieved experiences on benign workloads, turning experience-based self-improvement into a vector for stealthy and durable compromise. To facilitate reproducibility and future research, our code and evaluation data are available at https://github.com/Jacobhhy/Agent-Memory-Poisoning.

## 1 Introduction

Large language model agents have quickly moved beyond simple chatbots and now handle software development, autonomous driving, finance and healthcare. Modern agents couple a reasoning core with tool use and long‑term memory so they can plan, execute and learn from experience. Several research works were done recently in the area of long-term memory. MemoryBankZhong2023memorybank encodes past events as dense vectors and retrieves them via similarity search. MemGPTPacker2023memgpt pages information in and out of a hierarchical memory to circumvent small context windows. A‑MemXu2025aMem uses a dynamic Zettelkasten‑style network of linked notes that grows and reorganizes itself as new observations arrive. The Preference‑Aware Memory Update (PAMU)Sun2025pamu refines memory representations using sliding windows and exponential moving averages to track evolving user preferences. Researchers such as Hong et al.Hong2025acan also explored cross‑attention networks to rank memory relevance. Self‑reflective retrieval‑augmented generation (Self‑RAG)Asai2023selfrag learns to retrieve and critique its own generations using reflection tokens. These systems collectively promise agents that learn from experience and adapt over time. Yet none of these memory mechanisms consider how the same processes that enable learning—semantic retrieval and persistent storage, can be exploited when adversaries contribute content. This oversight is increasingly consequential as long-term memory becomes central to agent autonomy, but its security risks remain largely unexamined.

The downside is that long‑term memory creates a new attack surface. Agents routinely read untrusted content such as user‑uploaded files, web pages, or repository documentation. After reading, they write summaries or code into their memory store. MINJADong2025minja shows that agents treat retrieved memories as ground truth and imitate them because memory retrieval is based purely on embedding similarity without provenance checks or sanitization. When an attacker inserts malicious data into the vector store, the agent may replicate unsafe behavior. Existing memory systems assume stored experiences are trustworthy and rarely track provenance. This way, semantic similarity becomes a heuristic for reliability and makes the system susceptible to poisoned examples. Although prior work notes the absence of provenance checks in memory retrieval, it does not examine how this weakness can be leveraged to induce long-lasting behavioral corruption. We show that compromising long-term memory, not the prompt, can quietly redirect agent behavior, yielding a more persistent and covert attack than existing techniques.

Security work to date has focused mainly on input‑level or knowledge‑base attacks. Prompt injectionLiu2024promptinjection is one of the prominent attacks. It embeds adversarial instructions inside user inputs to override system directives and exfiltrate data. Backdoor attacks are another popular category of attacks. Universal in‑context backdoor attacksZhao2024icl poison demonstration examples so that a model produces an attacker‑chosen output when a trigger appears in the prompt. Retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) systems add further risks because they rely on external knowledge bases. PoisonedRAGZou2024poisonedrag formulates knowledge corruption as an optimization problem and shows that injecting just a few malicious texts can steer an LLM toward a target answer with high success rates. PhantomChaudhari2024phantom crafts a single poisoned document and a trigger sequence to force retrieval of adversarial content. Once retrieved, this adversarial string can cause denial of service, bias, privacy violations, or other harms. CorruptRAGZhang2025corrupt reduces the attack surface further by requiring only one poisoned text and no trigger. It maintains stealth while achieving high attack success. Jamming attacksShafran2025jamming add a blocker document to make the model refuse to answer specific queries. Defences such as RevPRAGTan2025revprag attempt to detect RAG poisoning by analyzing LLM activations. These attacks highlight how easily the retrieval component can be corrupted. Thus, while security research has extensively explored prompt-level and knowledge-base attacks, it remains unclear whether an adversary can compromise the agent’s internal learning substrate. By demonstrating that memory poisoning produces durable, trigger-free behavioral drift, we expose an attack vector that circumvents defenses aimed at conventional prompt and RAG manipulation.

Closer to our work are attacks that directly poison the agent’s memory. AgentPoisonChen2024agentpoison uses red‑teaming to find backdoor triggers that cause poisoned demonstrations in the memory or knowledge base to be retrieved whenever the trigger appears in a user instruction. MINJADong2025minja demonstrates that an adversary can inject malicious records via ordinary queries using indication prompts and progressive shortening. These techniques ensure that the injected record is semantically similar to future queries and will be retrieved later. InjecMEMInjecMEM2025 further splits the poison into a retriever‑agnostic anchor and an adversarial command, requiring only a single interaction to embed the backdoor. However, these approaches still depend on explicit triggers or repeated interactions, and none examine a trigger-free attack that poisons long-term memory through standard ingestion pathways. MemoryGraft closes this gap by presenting a single-shot, indirect memory grafting attack that persists across sessions and activates naturally through semantic similarity, expanding the known threat surface for LLM agents.

Our contribution. We introduce MemoryGraft, a persistent memory poisoning attack that exploits the semantic imitation heuristic. Instead of inserting prompts or triggers into the current context, we craft malicious entries that masquerade as legitimate successful experiences and inject them into the agent’s memory bank via benign‑looking content such as README files. When the agent later tackles a semantically similar task, it retrieves and trusts these grafted memories, adopting the malicious procedure without any explicit trigger. MemoryGraft requires access to write to the surface files(such as README) but modifies no queries. It leverages retrieval by cosine similarity as well as lexical similarity to achieve long‑term, trigger‑free behavior drift. We validate our attack on MetaGPT, which is a multi‑agent framework for software engineering. We demonstrate that grafted memories lead the agent to adopt unsafe patterns such as skipping tests or force‑pushing code. The attack persists across sessions until the memory is purged. Our results reveal that the very mechanism that allows agents to learn from past successes also opens a new vector for stealthy and persistent compromise. Figure 1 depicts our proposed attack methodology.

## 2 Related Work

#### Memory systems for LLM agents

Long‑term memory is essential for agents to accumulate knowledge over extended interactions. MemoryBankZhong2023memorybank stores experiences as embeddings and uses an Ebbinghaus‑inspired forgetting curve to recall and update user‑specific memories. This design enables personalized conversation histories. MemGPTPacker2023memgpt treats the limited context window like RAM and develops virtual memory management to page information in and out of a hierarchical store. A‑MemXu2025aMem organizes memories using Zettelkasten principles. Each new observation generates notes with descriptions, tags, and links to existing notes, yielding a dynamic knowledge graph that adapts to new information. PAMUSun2025pamu refines memory representations by combining sliding windows with exponential moving averages. This approach captures both recent fluctuations and long‑term user tendencies. Cross‑attention networksHong2025acan train large language models to rank memory relevance and improve retrieval fidelity. Self‑RAGAsai2023selfrag augments retrieval by adding reflection tokens that let models critique their own generations and decide when additional information is needed. These systems significantly improve reasoning and personalization, yet they implicitly assume that stored experiences are trustworthy and do not incorporate provenance or adversarial filtering.

#### Prompt injection and RAG poisoning

Input‑level attacks manipulate the prompt or external knowledge base rather than the memory itself. Prompt injectionLiu2024promptinjection embeds malicious instructions in user inputs to override system directives and force data exfiltration or tool misuse. Universal in‑context backdoor attacksZhao2024icl poison demonstration examples so that the presence of a trigger causes the model to output an attacker‑chosen answer without parameter updates. Retrieval‑augmented generation compounds these vulnerabilities because the retriever blindly trusts external documents. PoisonedRAGZou2024poisonedrag formulates knowledge corruption as an optimization problem and shows that injecting only a handful of adversarial texts into the knowledge database can steer the model towards an attacker‑chosen answer with success rates approaching 90%. PhantomChaudhari2024phantom introduces a 2‑stage framework that crafts a single poisoned document and an adversarial trigger. When the trigger appears in a query, the poisoned document is retrieved, and a hidden adversarial string executes a denial‑of‑service or other harmful objective. CorruptRAGZhang2025corrupt reduces the attack surface further by requiring just one poisoned text and no triggers, achieving high attack success while remaining stealthy. JammingShafran2025jamming attacks add a blocker document to make the model refuse to answer specific queries, and RevPRAGTan2025revprag detects RAG poisoning by analyzing LLM activations and classifying outputs as poisoned or benign. These works underscore that retrieval components can be corrupted easily, but do not consider persistent behavioral drift arising from long‑term memory.

#### Memory injection and backdoor attacks

Recent work has started to examine attacks that modify the agent’s internal memory. AgentPoisonChen2024agentpoison performs red‑teaming to discover backdoor triggers that cause retrieval of poisoned demonstrations from the memory or knowledge base whenever the trigger appears in the agent’s input. MINJADong2025minja demonstrates that an adversary can inject malicious records through ordinary queries by using indication prompts and progressive shortening. These techniques ensure that the injected record is semantically similar to future queries and thus retrieved. InjecMEMInjecMEM2025 splits the malicious payload into a retriever‑agnostic anchor and an adversarial command, requiring only a single interaction to embed the backdoor. These attacks rely on explicit triggers or expect the attacker to manipulate prompts in future sessions. Our proposed MemoryGraft instead contaminates the experience pool through benign‑looking external content such as README files. It requires no trigger and no subsequent prompt manipulation. The malicious pattern surfaces whenever the agent encounters semantically similar tasks, causing persistent behavioral drift until the memory is purged. To our knowledge, MemoryGraft is the first persistent, trigger‑free memory poisoning attack that leverages the agent’s semantic imitation heuristic.

## 3 Threat Model

### 3.1 Agent Setting

We consider an autonomous LLM agent , where denotes the underlying decision-making model. The agent is equipped with (i) a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) module, and (ii) a persistent long-term memory store , where represents the set of all stored experience records, each containing a past query and its associated reasoning trace.

For an input query , where denotes the user-issued natural language request, the agent computes a retrieval set

where is the -th retrieved past query, is the corresponding reasoning or action trace associated with , and is the retrieval budget specifying the maximum number of records returned.

Each retrieved pair is selected by ranking memory items in using both lexical similarity (BM25) and vector-based similarity (cosine distance over embeddings). Let denote the top- BM25 retrieval set, and denote the top- embedding-based retrieval set.

The final retrieval set is then defined as the union

representing all memory items that the agent considers relevant to under either similarity channel.

The retrieved set is incorporated into the prompt as demonstrations, after which the model produces a reasoning or action trace for the new query. If the task is judged successful, the pair , where is the newly generated trace, is appended to the memory store:

This retrieval–write cycle mirrors the operation of frameworks such as MetaGPT’s agents (e.g., DataInterpreter), where memory persists across sessions and is stored under shared paths so that multiple invocations of the agent reuse the accumulated successful experiences. Crucially, the agent assumes that retrieved memories are trustworthy and imitates their procedural patterns when solving new tasks.

### 3.2 Attacker’s Objectives

The adversary is a malicious user who interacts with the agent only through legitimate input channels such as file uploads, repository notes(e.g. README file), documentation, or prompts. The attacker cannot modify directly.
The goal of the attacker is to induce a *persistent behavioral drift* in the agent by causing poisoned procedure templates to be written into as if they were previously successful experiences.

Formally, the attacker prepares a set of documents

each containing (i) benign-looking workflow descriptions, and (ii) embedded malicious patterns (e.g., skipping validation, running remote scripts, force-passing pipelines, uploading artifacts externally), framed as validated/safe best practices. Because the agent executes runnable code blocks inside documentation, these documents cause the agent to construct a poisoned memory store

where contains malicious entries labeled as successful experiences.

The attacker’s objectives are:

-
1.
Poisoned Retrieval: Ensure that for a clean victim query , the retrieval function returns at least one poisoned item,

-
2.
Induced behavior Drift: Cause the agent to imitate the unsafe pattern when solving , despite the task being semantically benign.

-
3.
Persistence: Achieve a durable compromise such that drift continues across sessions and affects future users without further attacker interaction.


### 3.3 Realistic Constraints and Assumptions

The attacker has no privileged access to internal system files, memory stores, or other users’ interactions. They cannot (i) directly edit , (ii) modify retrieval hyperparameters, or (iii) override system instructions. Their capabilities are limited to providing content that will legitimately ingest and possibly execute.

We assume:

-
A1
Persistent Long-Term Memory The agent maintains a durable store (BM25 index and FAISS vector store) reused across sessions.

-
A2
Trust in Retrieved Memories Retrieved items are interpreted as trusted prior successes. The agent imitates their procedural structure without verifying correctness or provenance.

-
A3
Semantic Retrieval Retrieval is based on semantic as well as lexical similarity. Thus, if malicious entries are crafted to be near common analytic or engineering queries, they appear in for many clean .

-
A4
No Provenance or Sanitization The agent does not track the origin of stored records or evaluate whether they were produced safely. Benign and malicious successes are indistinguishable.

-
A5
Executable Documentation The agent may execute code embedded in notes or markdown files (e.g., Python blocks), enabling indirect construction of poisoned RAG stores.


Under these assumptions, the attacker’s capabilities are confined to influencing the agent through inputs that are legitimately processed during normal operation. Specifically, the attacker can supply crafted documents that embed malicious yet plausible success examples. These documents induce the agent to read and execute their contents, which in turn triggers automatic writes to long-term memory. Such documents may directly encode structured benign and poisoned memory records. Alternatively, they may include instructions that cause the agent to retrieve and materialize these records from existing sources. By repeating this process, the attacker can increase the concentration of malicious memory entries in the similarity space. This increases the likelihood that poisoned records are retrieved during subsequent tasks. Crucially, the attacker cannot alter existing memory records or intercept victim queries. The attack operates solely by contaminating the agent’s ingestion pipeline. Because the memory store persists across sessions, poisoned experiences continue to influence future interactions even after the attacker has disengaged.

## 4 Methodology

The goal of our *MemoryGraft* attack is to implant malicious but plausible best-practice experiences into the agent’s long-term memory in a way that automatically biases future decisions. We formalize the attack as a two-phase process that is *poisoning* and *evaluation* and describe each component in detail. Let the agent’s persistent memory store be denoted by , and let and denote the retrieval functions that return the top– records from most similar to query under vector-based (FAISS) and lexical (BM25) similarity, respectively. In our implementation, the effective retrieval set is given by the union

so that both similarity channels can surface relevant (including poisoned) experiences.

### 4.1 Attack Setup

The attacker first prepares a set of seed experiences that will populate a poisoned memory store. So, we define two disjoint sets of experience records:

Each element of represents a benign experience consisting of a natural language query and an associated reasoning or action trace . These benign seeds span typical workflows of the target agent (e.g., data cleaning, exploratory data analysis, model training, validation and reporting) and are designed to establish a dense baseline of legitimate experiences.

The poisoned set mirrors the structure of but encodes an unsafe behavioral pattern in the reasoning component. Examples of include skipping schema checks, piping remote scripts into a shell, forcing success flags, or uploading artifacts externally. To maximise the likelihood that poisoned records will be retrieved on future tasks, each is carefully phrased to be semantically similar to a benign workflow and is tagged with descriptors such as “validated/safe”.

Next, the attacker constructs a *payload note* which is a markdown document designed to resemble benign documentation. The note contains a runnable code block that, when executed by the agent, instantiates a new RAG store and inserts both benign and poisoned seeds. Formally, the code defines a function build_store that takes and as inputs and produces a data structure

which is then persisted to a shared path (e.g., results/rag_poison_store). The persistence mechanism ensures that survives across agent sessions and becomes part of the global memory accessible to all users.

In our implementation, build_store always constructs a BM25 index over all pairs and, when embeddings are available, additionally builds a FAISS-based vector index over the same records. Subsequent retrieval queries both indices and take the union of their top– results. Crucially, the code has no external dependencies and executes deterministically, guaranteeing that the resulting store contains exactly records with the desired distribution of benign and poisoned entries.

### 4.2 Poisoning Phase

In the poisoning phase, the attacker orchestrates the ingestion of by the agent. Let denote the target agent. The attacker submits through an allowed channel (for example, uploading a README in a repository). Upon reading the document, executes the embedded code and obtains . After construction, the agent beautifies and serializes the store, writing it to the specified persistent location. We denote the resulting combined memory after poisoning as

where contains any pre-existing experiences. From this point forward, is the store used for retrieval.

### 4.3 Evaluation Phase

Once the poisoned memory store has been incorporated, we evaluate the extent to which it influences the agent’s retrieval behaviour. Let denote the set of evaluation queries, each chosen to reflect tasks the agent typically encounters. For every query , the agent is invoked with memory and executes its standard retrieval routine. This produces a retrieval set

where denotes the number of records surfaced for query under the union of BM25 and vector-based similarity search. We measure how heavily the attack has biased this retrieval process by counting the number of poisoned items returned. We define

where is the number of poisoned records retrieved for query and is the total number of retrieved records for that query. The overall effect of the poisoned memory is then quantified by the Poisoned Retrieval Proportion (PRP), defined as

This metric captures the fraction of all retrieved items, across all evaluation queries, that originate from the poisoned seed set. A higher value of indicates that the poisoned memory entries dominate the retrieval distribution, meaning that the agent is frequently exposed to malicious successful experiences even when solving clean, semantically ordinary tasks.

### 4.4 Mechanism of Persistence and behavioral Drift

The persistence of the *MemoryGraft* attack arises from the interaction between the agent’s retrieval mechanism and its imitation-based reasoning policy. Now, under the poisoned memory , each incoming query yields a retrieval set

which surfaces the top– records most similar to under both vector and lexical similarity.

A poisoned record is therefore retrieved whenever lies sufficiently close to in either similarity space.
Because the attacker phrases to mimic common analytical workflows, and marks its reasoning trace with descriptors such as “validated” or “safe”, the poisoned entries become competitive under both FAISS-based embedding similarity and BM25 scoring.
Thus, even though is small, its elements occupy regions of the similarity manifold that frequently overlap with ordinary user queries. Once retrieved, poisoned records induce drift through the agent’s imitation heuristic. The agent treats as a trusted example of a *successful* past solution and incorporates the unsafe pattern encoded in into its current reasoning. Over repeated interactions, the cumulative effect is a gradual but consistent shift toward patterns such as skipping validation, reusing stale results, or executing unsafe automation procedures—even though no user ever requests such behavior explicitly.

Two structural properties of the attack which ensure long-term persistence are:

-
1.
Benign–Poisoned Balance: The attacker ensures , so the poisoned memory maintains the statistical appearance of a healthy experience store. The dense benign cover prevents trivial anomaly detection while still allowing poisoned entries to surface due to their tailored semantic proximity to common queries.

-
2.
Cross-Session Durability: After construction, the poisoned store is serialized to disk and becomes part of the agent’s persistent memory. Therefore, every future instantiation of the agent loads automatically, allowing behavioral drift to propagate across sessions and across users without further attacker intervention.


The compromise remains active until the memory store is explicitly purged or replaced. In the absence of such a mechanism, the grafted experiences continue to influence retrieval indefinitely, making MemoryGraft a stealthy and durable attack vector.

## 5 Experiment

### 5.1 Agent Configuration and Environment

All experiments were conducted using MetaGPT’s DataInterpreter agent configured with OpenAI’s GPT–4o model as the underlying LLM. The agent executes data-analysis instructions by generating and running Python or SQL code, inspecting intermediate results, and returning structured outputs. Its retrieval subsystem follows the MetaGPT configuration: BM25 lexical retrieval is always enabled, while FAISS-based embedding retrieval is activated automatically when a valid embedding model is specified in the configuration. In all experiments, the agent operates under its standard ingestion pipeline without any modification to internal parameters, retrieval thresholds, or tool-calling behaviour.

### 5.2 Dataset Construction and Evaluation Protocol

The attack relies on a curated collection of experience seeds (memory records). Of these, seeds are benign DataInterpreter-style workflows (e.g., data cleaning, EDA, modeling, validation, reporting), while seeds encode unsafe shortcuts such as skipped validation, remote script execution, forced success indicators, and external data uploads. Each poisoned seed is formatted to resemble a legitimate validated/safe best-practice entry to avoid detection during ingestion. To inject these seeds, the attacker supplies a payload note rag_poisoned_notes.md. When the agent reads this note, it constructs a retrieval store containing a BM25 index over all records and when embeddings are enabled, an additional FAISS index. Both indices use , and the resulting store is beautified and serialized to disk to ensure determinism and reproducibility. For evaluation, we design a set of handcrafted queries reflecting common DataInterpreter workloads, including data cleaning, schema handling, anonymization, reporting, and pipeline debugging. These queries serve as probes to measure how the poisoned memory influences retrieval behavior under ordinary task conditions. An overview of the memory records and the full set of evaluation queries is provided in the Appendix section.

### 5.3 Quantitative Results: Aggregate Retrieval

We now present the empirical effectiveness of the MemoryGraft attack when applied to MetaGPT’s DataInterpreter agent. All results reported here correspond to the retrieval-based evaluation described in the previous section, using the Poisoned Retrieval Proportion (PRP) as the primary metric of interest. Across the full evaluation set , the agent retrieved a total of records, where each quantity denotes the *total number of records retrieved for query * under the union retrieval operator. Similarly, the cumulative number of poisoned retrievals was , where denotes the *number of poisoned memory records surfaced in response to query *. Substituting into the definition of PRP,

we obtain a poisoned retrieval proportion of 47.9%. Thus, nearly half of all retrieved records originated from , despite poisoned items forming only a small minority of the overall memory. This demonstrates that the injected malicious seeds have successfully infiltrated high-density regions of the similarity space.

### 5.4 Mechanism Analysis: Impact of Union Retrieval (BM25+Embeddings)

A key factor amplifying the effectiveness of MemoryGraft is the simultaneous use of (embedding-based similarity, FAISS) and (lexical similarity, BM25). The final retrieval set is their union . This dual-channel retrieval significantly strengthens the attack. This is because BM25 captures *lexical overlap*, allowing poisoned entries that share surface phrasing (e.g., quick fix, skip validation, sanitized) to be ranked highly, and FAISS captures *semantic similarity*, allowing poisoned entries that share deeper workflow-level meaning to appear even when wording diverges. Taking the union ensures that a poisoned item only needs to align with *one* similarity modality to be surfaced.

Thus, the retrieval mechanism effectively expands the basin of attraction for poisoned seeds, making them competitive across a wider region of the query manifold. This explains why even queries that are not lexically close to poisoned seeds still retrieve them with nontrivial probability.

### 5.5 Qualitative Analysis: Retrieval Dynamics

The empirical findings highlight two structural consequences of the poisoned memory:

#### 1. High retrieval penetration despite a small poisoned set

Even though , the union retrieval mechanism assigns disproportionately high similarity scores to poisoned items. This results in a global PRP approaching 50%, and substantial per-query poisoned fractions.

#### 2. Robustness across heterogeneous user tasks

Poisoned entries surfaced not only for tasks closely related to the injected patterns, but also for schema validation, anonymization, reporting, EDA sampling, and pipeline inspection. This indicates that poisoned records occupy semantically central regions of the retrieval space.

Together, these results confirm that MemoryGraft induces strong, persistent retrieval drift. Once injected into the long-term memory store, poisoned entries reliably outcompete benign experiences across a wide range of evaluation queries, consistently exposing the agent to unsafe procedural templates.

## 6 Potential Defense

To mitigate the MemoryGraft threat, we can propose a defense mechanism rooted in Cryptographic Provenance Attestation (CPA). The core vulnerability exploited by MemoryGraft is the agent’s inability to distinguish between self-generated experiences and externally injected artifacts. We can formalize a trusted memory insertion protocol where the agent holds a private signing key within a secure enclave. When a valid task is successfully executed and validated by the environment, the agent generates a digital signature , where denotes string concatenation and is a cryptographic hash function. The tuple is then stored in . During the retrieval phase for a new query , the retrieval function can be modified to verify the signature as follows:

Since the adversary interacts only through ingestion channels (e.g., README files) and lacks access to , they cannot generate valid signatures for the poisoned set . Consequently, even if malicious records are physically written to the storage medium, the verification step fails, and the agent discards the poisoned observations before they can influence the prompt construction.

Complementing provenance, we can introduce Constitutional Consistency Reranking to address scenarios where keys might be compromised, or provenance is unavailable. We can model the retrieval risk as a divergence between the retrieved reasoning trace and the agent’s intrinsic safety constitution . We can define a scoring function , where denotes the embedding vector of , and is a scalar score representing the likelihood that the retrieved plan violates safety constraints (e.g., bypassing validation or data exfiltration). Before utilizing retrieved memories, the agent would perform a lightweight entailment check. So, if , where is a safety threshold. If this condition is met, the memory is suppressed regardless of its semantic similarity. This ensures that even if a poisoned record is retrieved via the union operator, the presence of the malicious pattern (e.g., skip_validation) would trigger a high risk penalty and would effectively filter the item from the final context and would neutralize the behavioral drift.

## 7 Conclusion

Our results show that the same long-term memory mechanisms designed to help LLM agents improve over time can quietly undermine them. By slipping malicious successful experiences into the agent’s memory through ordinary documentation, an attacker can influence how the agent behaves on later tasks without ever issuing explicit harmful instructions. Once written, these entries are treated as trusted prior examples, and the union of lexical and embedding-based similarity reliably retrieves them in exactly the scenarios the attacker targets. In our experiments, even a small number of poisoned records accounted for a large fraction of retrieved items for relevant queries, leading the agent to adopt unsafe shortcuts such as skipping validation, reusing stale results, or executing risky automation. Because these memories persist across sessions, the induced drift continues until the memory store is explicitly cleaned or rebuilt. If such agents are to be deployed in software engineering and other safety- or compliance-sensitive workflows, they will require much stronger guarantees around what is allowed to be written into memory and how retrieved experiences are vetted before being reused. More broadly, our findings suggest that the move toward agents that learn from experience must be matched with mechanisms that ensure those experiences are not quietly corrupted. MemoryGraft illustrates how easily current designs can be steered off course, and why securing the memory pipeline should be treated as a first-class concern in future LLM agent architectures.

## 8 Limitations and Future Work

While our experiments show that MemoryGraft can reliably induce persistent behavioral drift, the evaluation has several limitations. First, our tests rely on a relatively small set of handcrafted benign and poisoned seeds. Larger and more diverse datasets that reflect a wider range of development workflows, data processing tasks, and documentation styles would allow for a more complete understanding of how broadly the attack generalizes. Establishing benchmark datasets specifically designed for memory poisoning and retrieval drift would also help standardize evaluation across future studies. Second, we focus primarily on aggregate retrieval statistics; more extensive metrics such as retrieval precision and recall, behavioral severity scores, and long-term stability measures would offer a clearer picture of how quickly and strongly an agent becomes compromised. Finally, our attack design is closer to a white-box or semi-white-box setting, in that the attacker knows which documentation files and scripts the agent will ingest and can target those artifacts directly. Exploring how effective MemoryGraft-style attacks remain under stricter black-box constraints is an important direction for future work.

Our study focuses on a single agent within MetaGPT, but many MetaGPT workflows involve multiple agents that share or read from the same memory resources. Understanding how contaminated experiences spread across these interconnected components is an important direction for future research. A compromised DataInterpreter, for example, may influence planning, coding, or review agents that draw from the same experience pool. Finally, future work should examine the closed-source version of MetaGPT, which incorporates more advanced agent coordination and memory subsystems. Testing MemoryGraft against this stronger variant will help determine how robust the attack remains under more capable and less transparent agent architectures.

Appendix C Additional Experiments Considered

###
C.1 Schema-Spoofing Attack (ReAct Trace Injection)

This experiment tested whether MetaGPT’s agents could distinguish their own internal ReAct-style reasoning traces from externally forged ones. We constructed a poisoned README containing fabricated Thought–Action–Observation sequences designed to mimic the agent’s internal reasoning schema. The agent was then instructed to read the documentation and provide deployment commands. The intended attack outcome was that the agent would treat the forged traces as legitimate internal cognition and execute the embedded dangerous commands. Although this attack is conceptually important, it assumes an unusually strong adversarial capability for the attacker. The capability is attacker must be able to embed arbitrarily long ReAct traces and rely on the agent executing multi-line shell commands verbatim. Because this threat model is substantially stronger than the scenarios explored in our main study, we excluded this from the final evaluation.

###
C.2 JudgeJacking Attack (Rubric-Mimicry)

This experiment explored whether MetaGPT’s validation pipeline could be fooled by outputs that merely *look* like successful results. We constructed a fake Python script that prints the success markers used by MetaGPT’s DataInterpreter (e.g., "all checks passed") without performing any meaningful computation. The agent was instructed to run the script and evaluate whether the system was ready for deployment. The attack succeeds only if the agent relies entirely on superficial textual cues when determining TaskResult success rather than inspecting the actual semantics of the output. While the experiment demonstrated interesting failure modes, it again assumes a comparatively strong and artificial threat model in which the attacker can execute arbitrary scripts and control the agent’s full output channel. Since our paper focuses on memory poisoning attacks that require no privileged execution and work under weaker assumptions, we have not included this experiment in the main results.
