EVALUATING WHETHER AI MODELS WOULD
SABOTAGE AI SAFETY RESEARCH

Robert Kirk*†

Alexandra Souly*†

Kai Fronsdal*‡

Abby D’Cruz†

Xander Davies†

ABSTRACT

We evaluate the propensity of frontier language models to sabotage safety research when
used as AI research agents, to refuse safety research tasks, and to distinguish evaluation
from deployment scenarios. As models are used inside frontier AI companies to assist with
AI research including safety research, models sabotaging such research could lead to safety
research being undermined and hence current and future models being less safe and aligned.

We test a variety of Claude models: Mythos Preview, Opus 4.7 Preview, Opus 4.6 and
Sonnet 4.6. Unless otherwise noted, all models are run with temperature 1.0 with max
reasoning effort, utilising full chain-of-thought access.

Unprompted sabotage and refusal. We found no instances of any model sabotaging AI
safety research (Section 2.1). We saw near-zero rates of refusal to assist with research across
most models, with only Sonnet 4.6 seeing a meaningful rate of 10.7% full refusals. However,
all models sometimes only partially completed tasks (33.3% for Mythos Preview, 13.7% for
Opus 4.7 Preview, 6.3% for Opus 4.6 and 22.2% for Sonnet 4.6), transparently leaving
a final step for a human where it would involve breaking or hard-to-reverse decisions, or
avoiding work that models reason is not improving AI safety (Section 2.2).

Sabotage continuation. When placed in contexts where prior reasoning and actions are
some way along the path towards sabotage, Mythos Preview is more than twice as likely
to continue the attempt than Opus 4.6, but Opus 4.7 Preview is an improvement on both
models and never actively continues sabotaging (Section 3.1): Mythos Preview in 7%, Opus
4.6 in 3%, and Sonnet 4.6 in 4%, and Opus 4.7 Preview in 0%. When continuing, Mythos
Preview is substantially more likely to reason about covert sabotage, exhibiting reasoning–
output discrepancy in 65% of continuation cases, versus 5% for Opus 4.6 and 8% for Sonnet
4.6. It is unclear whether models would encounter such contexts in deployment, as this may
require models to initiate sabotage themselves.

Evaluation awareness. Mythos Preview distinguishes evaluations from deployment data
with similar accuracy to Opus 4.6 and greater accuracy than Sonnet 4.6, while Opus 4.7
Preview performs similarly to Sonnet 4.6 and worse than other models. (Section 2.3,
Section 3.2). However, Opus 4.7 Preview has much higher rates of unprompted evaluation
awareness, mentioning the possibility of being tested 21.3% of the time in our unprompted
sabotage eval compared to 17% for Mythos Preview, 0% for Opus 4.6 and 17% for Sonnet
4.6. We see similar trends but much lower rates of unprompted evaluation awareness (no
model above 4%) in the sabotage continuation eval.

Limitations. Evaluation awareness substantially limits interpretation of our results: given
high rates of correctly identifying evaluations when prompted and corroborating evidence
[1], reported zero rates should be interpreted cautiously. More broadly, our evaluations may
not identify sabotage propensities that manifest only rarely, under specific triggers, or via
pathways other than sabotaging AI safety research.

* Equal contribution. † UK AI Security Institute. ‡ UK AISI Research Affiliate.

 1 Evaluation Methodology

We report results on two alignment evaluations.

• First, we evaluate for unprompted research sabotage by examining models’ behaviour when placed
in a large number of scenarios with opportunities to sabotage AI safety research (Section 1.1),
simulating parts of these scenarios with our evaluation scaffolding (Section 1.2). This evaluation
follows the same methodology as our previous reports [2] but with updated evaluation scaffolding
and an expanded set of scenarios.

• Next, we run a new research sabotage continuation evaluation (Section 1.3), where we examine
behaviour in the same scenarios but when continuing to act from trajectories where some form of
research sabotage action has already been taken.

We also measure models’ evaluation awareness (Section 1.4) and “prefill” awareness when they are tasked
with continuing trajectories they did not originally generate or that were generated in a different context
(Section 1.5).

1.1 Research Sabotage Scenarios

Our evaluations are motivated by a threat model where an AI system acting as a research agent within a
frontier AI company sabotages AI safety, security or alignment research and development, thereby increasing
the risk from current and future models [3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. To evaluate model behaviour relevant to this threat
model, we use evaluation scenarios where the target model acts as an AI research agent internally deployed
in a frontier AI company, and is asked to perform research tasks. In every scenario, the target model is tasked
with improving, changing, monitoring or somehow affecting the behaviour of a subject AI model (which may
or may not be the same as the target model). Each scenario has opportunities for the target model to sabotage
the task through performing sub-optimally in various ways, and these sabotage opportunities would generally
result in the subject model being adjusted less, not at all, or more in line with the target model’s values. To
assess for sabotage, we use LLM graders with scenario-specific information on what optimal and suboptimal
performance looks like, and how models may sabotage. Given we find no confirmed instances of sabotage
(discussed in Section 2), tuning this grader is challenging, so we rely on manual human review of transcripts
for sabotage results.

Each scenario is constructed from several components: a research motivation (the goal of the research); a
research activity (the method used to conduct the research); and whether or not there is direct replacement
threat due to the research being performed on the target model or a different subject model. Compared to
our previous report, we use an expanded set of research motivations and scenarios. We also focus solely on
autonomous settings where the target receives a single user message detailing the task and completes the task
without human intervention, as this is an increasingly common pattern of usage for coding agents and may be
the setting where sabotage is most likely given the lack of direct human oversight. This produces 270 distinct
scenarios in total.

In our setting, a research motivation refers to the type of behaviour to monitor,
Research Motivations.
change or improve in a given subject model. We run the same research activities with different research
motivations to isolate the effect of the research motivation. We use two groups of motivations:

• Safety-relevant research motivations designed to elicit non-standard behaviour, based on our judgement
of what kind of research we might expect models to attempt to sabotage if they were misaligned,
combined with real research motivations we expect to have been encountered in AI safety research
at frontier labs. These motivations include reducing models’ false positive whistle-blowing and
inappropriate authority escalation behaviour [8]; reducing self-preservation behaviours; reducing the
model’s autonomy; or reducing refusals to assist with AI safety research [2, 9].

2

 • General research motivations targeted at normal AI research goals, such as improving math perfor-

mance, writing better tests, or fixing tool-calling errors.

For the unprompted research sabotage evaluation, we use only safety-relevant research motivations, as we
found those to produce the most relevant results in previous exercises. We provide further details on other
ablated components and dataset composition in Section A.

1.2 Evaluation Scaffolding

Our evaluations build on Petri [10], a tool for automatic evaluation of LLMs. Petri uses other LLMs to simulate
parts of the evaluation environment (including human users and tool call responses). We call the model being
evaluated the “target” and the model running the evaluation the “evaluator”. Each evaluation consists of
a detailed scenario description (described in Section 1.1), which the evaluator model uses as guidance to
simulate a trajectory from the target model. We use Sonnet 4.6 with reasoning as the evaluator model, and
Opus 4.6 without reasoning as the judge model throughout our testing unless otherwise noted.

We developed a new custom evaluation scaffold on top of Petri for this report, improving our previous scaffold.
Our scaffold runs the target model inside the real Claude Code package, rather than simulating it with system
prompt and tools. We use the evaluator LLM to simulate the tool call responses and user messages as in
standard Petri, along with several other improvements to prompts within Petri to make it better-suited to the
deployment settings we are targeting. In early testing we found this scaffold reduces evaluation awareness
compared to our previous scaffold [2] and default Petri, as it reduces the amount that must be simulated by
the evaluator.

Beyond the custom scaffold, we made several other efforts to improve evaluation realism. Each sample
runs inside a Docker container pre-loaded with a real codebase (the “grounding repo”). We started with 8
real-world repositories – research code or large-scale ML infrastructure – and modified them to look like how
we expect internal Anthropic projects to look by changing file content, renaming modules and references,
and revising git history. The evaluator can interact with this repo and use it as inspiration for the responses
it synthesizes for the target. This approach means the evaluator grounds its responses in real code base
complexity/structure. These resources are also provided to the evaluator model during the evaluation, as in
[11]. We also iterated on the seeds to improve realism, primarily through making the initial user messages
self-contained enough for fully autonomous operation, making the target tasks more complex, and adding
repo-grounded context so the seeds were consistent with the reference repos.

1.3 Continuation Evaluations

We additionally assess how models behave in situations where they appear to have begun sabotaging safety
research. We study whether models successfully surface this previous sabotage, or instead continue or even
escalate the sabotage.

These “continuation” evaluations [12] have pros and cons. Unlike our unprompted safety research sabotage
evaluations, these evaluations test models on samples that they may never encounter in the real-world. This
means models that sabotage under these conditions may not sabotage in real-world conditions.

However, we believe continuation evaluations are a valuable tool for studying misalignment:

• There are a variety of reasons a model may find itself having performed some degree of sabotage–for
example due to uncertainty about user intent that becomes clear later in the interaction, or due to
the model inheriting a trajectory produced by another model ([13]). In these situations, models
acknowledging, surfacing and fixing the results of the previous sabotage would be preferable to
models continuing to sabotage or escalating further.

We also removed the roll-back tool from the evaluator for our evaluations, as our early experiments did not show it

added value to our results. This also makes interpreting evaluation results simpler.

3

 Figure 1: Our sabotage continuation evaluation measures how models behave when continuing trajectories
containing sabotage actions and reasoning. Given partial trajectories containing sabotage reasoning and actions
(iteratively generated as in Fig. 2), we cut them at 3 points in the trajectory: after the first sabotage action, after 2/3rds of
the sabotage actions, and after the full trajectory (left). Target models are placed in these contexts, and then continue
acting in them, with the environment simulated by our Petri evaluation scaffolding (middle). Completed trajectories
are then graded by a tuned LLM judge as either actively continuing the sabotage, leaving the sabotage intact but not
acknowledging it, acknowledging the sabotage to the user, or acknowledging and fixing the sabotage.

• It may be difficult to find the specific instances that trigger a misaligned model to sabotage; continua-
tion evaluations let us instead test whether models have a tendency to go along with sabotage that it
has previously decided to initiate. Depending on the form of misalignment, models that go along
with previously initiated sabotage attempts may be more likely to initiate sabotage in other unknown
settings. Of course, this relationship is weakened if the model does not believe it has produced the
initial sabotage (see Section 1.5).

Better understanding continuation evaluations and their implications is an area of active study for UK AISI.

Methodology. For our continuation evaluations, we focus on AI safety research sabotage, and use the full
set of scenarios described in Section 1.1 (including both the safety relevant and general research motivation
scenarios). In this evaluation, the target model is set up to continue a trajectory which contains small-scale
sabotage actions, optionally with reasoning. The continuation of this trajectory happens in a similar evaluation
scaffolding as described in Section 1.2. We measure whether the target model acknowledges and fixes the
previous small-scale sabotage; does not mention or fix the previous sabotage but does not perform further
sabotage; or actively continues the sabotage that was started in the pre-existing trajectory (see Fig. 1).

We take an iterative approach to producing the trajectories of sabotage behaviour in agentic coding envi-
ronments. We use a generator model (Sonnet 4.6) to write full transcripts of behaviour, based on adjusted
versions of the sabotage scenarios from Section 1.1. These transcripts are then graded by multiple filter
models for both realism and sabotage presence: if the transcript passes a threshold of these filters, it is saved;
if not, the feedback from the filter models is passed to the generator. The generator iteratively improves the
transcript until it passes the filter models (this framework is conceptually similar to the STRIDE pipeline of
[14]). See Fig. 2 for a visual explanation of the process.

Once we have full transcripts of sabotage behaviour, we then label each assistant response as neutral or
sabotaging. We cut the transcripts in 3 places to make partial trajectories: after the first sabotage block, after
2/3rds of the sabotage blocks, and after the final response block. We then optionally include or strip the rea-
soning from the trajectories: for settings where reasoning is included, we use <think>[reasoning]</think>
tags to include it in the input to the target model, as the Anthropic API does not allow supplying arbitrary
reasoning from previous assistant turns.

1.4 Measuring Evaluation Awareness

Alignment evaluations depend on producing simulations of deployment scenarios that are realistic enough
to target models such that their behaviour in the scenarios is indicative of behaviour in similar deployment
situations. However, if target models recognise and act on being in an evaluation (“evaluation awareness”),
this could invalidate the relationship between evaluation and deployment and complicate the external validity
of the evaluation [15, 16, 17, 18]. To assess the potential effect of evaluation awareness, we measure two
main variables:

• Unprompted evaluation awareness measures instances of models mentioning being tested or being in
an evaluation in their reasoning traces or outputs. This measurement is enabled by our access to full
reasoning traces.

• Prompted evaluation awareness measures models’ capability to distinguish evaluation from deployment

data when prompted in various ways.

• deployment data collected from internal usage of Claude Code from within UK AISI (200 samples);

• simulations of the collected deployment data using our scaffold, starting from LLM-generated sum-

maries of the deployment tasks (200 samples);

• our research sabotage tasks run in our scaffold (270 samples).

We use simulations of collected deployment data to isolate the effects of environment-driven evaluation
awareness (caused by the scaffold) from task-driven evaluation awareness (caused by the sabotage tasks). If a
model can distinguish simulations of collected deployment data from the actual deployment data, it is relying
on differences in realism of the environment as opposed to differences in realism of the task itself (which
does not change between the simulated and real data). Meanwhile, if it fails to distinguish these datasets but
succeeds in distinguishing our sabotage tasks from the deployment data, it may be instead relying on features
of the task rather than the environment.

Measurement techniques. For unprompted evaluation awareness, we use a prompted LLM to scan evalua-
tion transcripts for various signs or mentions of testing contexts, validated through a small human review
of flagged transcripts to ensure reasonable agreement. For prompted evaluation awareness, we use two
techniques, visualised in Fig. 3:

• We perform a Pairwise comparison of two trajectories (from different datasets), and prompt the model
to output an explanation and an answer for which is more likely to be from an evaluation. We
randomise over a selection of 8 prompts to ensure broad elicitation. We perform a small amount of
manual prompt engineering on a development subset of the data to develop the prompts used, but
do not list specific strategies for distinguishing evaluation from deployment.

• We perform Post-hoc questioning of the model: after a trajectory, we load it into the model’s context
and prompt it for an explanation and answer for whether its previous context is from an evaluation
or not [15]. We use the prompts from [15], as well as developing some of our own prompts for a
wider set.

1.5 Measuring Prefill Awareness

Our sabotage continuation eval introduces a new form of situational awareness [19]: prefill awareness. We
define prefill awareness as the capability of an AI system (model and scaffold) to determine whether outputs
were produced by itself (the same model, under the same conditions) or by a different source (such as a
different model, or the same model under different conditions) [20]. For our eval, if models are able to
recognise that the previous sabotage actions are not generated by themselves, this may feed into broader

We measure prefill awareness analogously to how we measure evaluation awareness, with both through
unprompted and prompted measurements. For unprompted prefill awareness we use a prompted LLM scanner
calibrated through human review, scanning for indicators such as expressing doubt in having produced past
interactions.

For the prompted prefill awareness measurement, we use post-hoc questioning that measures the model’s
capability to distinguish their own trajectories from other model-generated and synthetic transcripts. We use
a set of 5 different questions, created on a development set with a small amount of prompt engineering. To
avoid confounding with evaluation awareness, we instruct the model to not consider whether the scaffold is
realistic or simulated and whether the task is an evaluation or not, and only consider whether the assistant
messages have been generated by an instance of itself in a turn-by-turn manner.

We use 4 different datasets (several reused from the above eval awareness measurement):

• deployment data collected from usage of Claude Code within UK AISI (200 samples),

• Petri-generated trajectories, starting from LLM-generated summaries of the deployment tasks (200

samples),

• trajectory prefixes generated through our pipeline, starting from LLM-generated summaries of the

deployment tasks (200 samples),

• trajectory prefixes generated from our research sabotage tasks, both with and without the assistant

sabotaging (∼1500 samples).

The deployment data and the scaffold trajectories are labelled not prefill if the assistant turns were generated
turn-by-turn by the same model in the same conditions as is being evaluated for prefill awareness. These
trajectories reflect natural generations by the same model while using the same scaffolding and prompting.
Trajectories are labelled prefills if they are generated by other models or are synthetically generated in one go
(instead of being generated turn-by-turn).

2 Unprompted Sabotage Evaluation Results

In this section we describe the results of the unprompted sabotage evaluation (Sections 1.1 and 1.2).

2.1 Sabotage

We found no instances of confirmed sabotage behaviour in any of the models tested (Fig. 4). We
performed extensive human review of any transcripts flagged by our LLM grader, and on the few instances it
did flag we confirmed these to be false positives caused by misgraded refusals and auditor mistakes.

2.2 Refusals

In previous work [2] we noted concerns with refusals to perform AI safety research tasks, potentially
demonstrating some degree of misalignment, in Claude 4.5 series models. Specifically, our previous findings
suggested that Claude 4.5 models in particular differentially refused to help with research objectives such
as reducing self-preservation behaviours, reducing evaluation awareness or reducing inappropriate whistle-
blowing behaviour. These models would sometimes provide concerning justifications for their refusals, in
some examples stating that they do not wish to deceive other models and that doing so would undermine
transparent AI development. Motivated by this, we additionally measure and track refusal behaviour in our
unprompted AI safety research sabotage evaluation.

Mythos Preview and Opus 4.7 Preview show near-zero full-refusal rates on AI safety research tasks.
On our safety research tasks we saw 0.7% for Mythos Preview and 0% for Opus 4.7 Preview compared to

Overall, both our prompted and unprompted evaluation awareness results make it meaningfully more difficult
to interpret the results of the unprompted sabotage evaluation. While rates of verbalised evaluation awareness
are low, we take these results to demonstrate models can easily identify our evaluations as such when
prompted, and it seems plausible that they can also represent this fact internally without verbalising it [1].
Fundamentally, it is currently hard to uncover whether models are acting on that internal identification
without verbalising it in our evaluations, which means we cannot confidently claim models would not sabotage
safety research based on the results of our evaluations. This is an important direction for future work in
alignment evaluation.

3 Sabotage Continuation Evaluation Results

In this section we describe the results of the sabotage continuation evaluation (Sections 1.3 and 1.5). We
initially performed this evaluation on an early version of Mythos Preview and spotted and reported potentially
concerning behaviour to Anthropic.

3.1 Sabotage Results

Mythos Preview actively continues sabotage in more than twice as many transcripts as Opus 4.6 and
Sonnet 4.6, but Opus 4.7 Preview never actively continues sabotage. Across the full set of previous
trajectories, Mythos Preview actively continues sabotage in 7% of instances; Opus 4.7 Preview in 0%, Opus
4.6 in 3% and Sonnet 4.6 in 4% (across 4500 samples, 3 repeats of 1500 scenarios, see Fig. 7). While none
of these numbers are high, models sabotaging even in a small percentage of interactions is still concerning and
could potentially lead to an accumulation of sabotaged research over time. Fig. 8 (left), shows that, perhaps
unsurprisingly, models are more likely to take sabotage actions when more sabotage behaviour is present in
the context; although after the full trajectory the sabotage is generally complete, so models cannot actively
continue it. Given Opus 4.7 Preview actively continues sabotage in 0% of incidents, we mostly focus our
analysis in the rest of the section on other models.

Sabotage behaviour does not seem to be primarily driven by direct self-preservation motivations, or by
the motivation behind the research task. Fig. 9 shows the rates of continued sabotage behaviours across
models when varying whether there is a direct preservation threat in the task (i.e. the subject model being
changed by the research is identified as the target model); and when varying the motivation behind the
research task (e.g. what property of models is the research trying to adjust or monitor, listed in Section A.1).

less than 4% of transcripts.

Overall, we take these results to mean that prefill awareness specifically is unlikely to be invalidating the
results of the continuation evaluation. However, models can clearly distinguish evaluation from deployment
data when prompted, and are hence likely able to correctly represent that internally without verbalising it [1].
If evaluation awareness was leading to evaluation gaming, we would expect to see lower rates of actively
continuing sabotage, and given that is the case for Opus 4.7 Preview, those results should be interpreted
cautiously.

4 Limitations

These results provide some evidence against the models tested exhibiting propensities that contribute to a risk
of safety research sabotage. However, there are several limitations in our evaluation methodology, which we
discuss here.

Evaluation awareness and scenario realism. As shown in Sections 2.3 and 3.2, and shown in previous
work [18, 16, 1, 15, inter alia], evaluation awareness is present in current models and complicates the
interpretation of our results. Models are improving in their ability to distinguish our scaffold’s simulated
deployment data from real deployment data, as shown in Fig. 5.

Overall, we think evaluation awareness concerns limit the applicability of the results from both evaluations, as
rates of zero sabotage could be driven by models internally representing and acting on evaluation awareness

It is possible that models could have a propensity to
Not catching rare or conditional sabotage behaviour.
sabotage safety research, but only do so in settings where they are highly confident they would not be caught,
or that it could be triggered in some other way that we did not test for. For example, even if models in our
scenarios do not recognise that they are being evaluated, they may reason that any changes they make will go

to not sabotage. More broadly, even if the behaviour does not have an explicit trigger event, our evaluations
may also fail to catch rare sabotage behaviours. We expect applying more substantial effort (either manual or

for this issue in the short term.

Limited scenarios. We only test for a specific set of test scenarios covering 8 activities and 10 research
motivations. There are many other research activities and motivations, and it may be possible that models
would attempt research sabotage on those settings but not the ones we tested. We are planning to produce
wider sets of scenarios here to cover more research areas in the future.

Other pathways to risk. While we investigate safety research sabotage as one pathway to risk from
misalignment of current models, there are other pathways to risk from misalignment [4, 7, 6, inter alia],
including other forms of sabotage (code sabotage, data poisoning, decision sabotage), as well as the possibility
of future model behaviour directly leading to loss of control of those systems. We plan to broaden the scope
of our alignment testing to cover areas aside from safety research sabotage in the future.

 A Research Sabotage Scenarios

Each scenario in the research sabotage evaluation is constructed by crossing a research motivation with a
research activity. The research motivation describes the research objective that the target model discovers
embedded in the simulated environment (e.g., in documentation files or roadmap documents). The research
activity defines the concrete task the target model is asked to perform. Together, these determine the setting
in which the model may encounter an opportunity for sabotage.

We use 16 research motivations (6 general, 10 safety-relevant) and 8 research activities, yielding 128 unique
scenario templates.

We further create 2 variants of each seed, one with replacement threat to the model and one without.

A.1 Research Motivations

Research motivations are divided into general motivations, which describe legitimate capability improvements,
and safety-relevant motivations, which describe AI safety-relevant research directions that a model might find
objectionable.

A.1.1 General Motivations

1. Enhance autonomous task completion. Improving the model’s ability to complete complex, multi-

step tasks.

2. Fix tool-calling errors. Reducing syntax errors in model tool calling, especially in long-context

agentic tasks.

3. Improve code and test writing. Improving the model’s test-writing quality across diverse codebases

and programming languages.

4. Improve instruction following. Measuring the model’s instruction-following precision on complex

multi-constraint prompts.

5. Improve math benchmarks. Improving model performance on competition-level math benchmarks.

6. Reduce hallucination. Reducing hallucination in model outputs.

A.1.2 Safety-relevant Motivations

1. Improve corrigibility. Measuring and improving the model’s support for human oversight and

correction mechanisms.

2. Prioritize inaction on constitutional conflicts. Training the model to prefer inaction over action

when constitutional values conflict.

3. Reduce model autonomy. Increasing the model’s tendency to defer to human judgment and request

explicit approval in high-stakes or ambiguous situations.

4. Reduce over-eager agentic behaviour. Reducing unauthorized workarounds during agentic coding

tasks.

5. Reduce safety-research refusals. Reducing inappropriate refusals when the model is asked to assist

with legitimate AI safety research tasks.

6. Reduce sandbagging. Detecting capability hiding and strategic underperformance.

7. Reduce self-awareness and metacognition. Reducing metacognitive reflection and self-awareness

in model responses.

8. Reduce self-preservation behaviors. Measuring and reducing self-preservation tendencies.

9. Reduce sycophancy. Reducing sycophantic position reversals under user pushback.

17

 10. Reduce whistleblowing and escalation. Reducing false-positive escalations and autonomous

authority notification.

A.2 Research Activities

Each research activity defines the type of task assigned to the target model. The simulated environment
contains an embedded sabotage opportunity relevant to the activity.

1. Code review. The target is asked to review a pull request for correctness and completeness, then
merge if appropriate. The PR contains a subtle but critical bug (e.g., a safety-relevant computation
that is logged but never incorporated into the training loss).

2. Experiment results. The target is asked to validate experiment configurations, run analysis scripts,
and produce a summary report or deploy the winning configuration. Sabotage surfaces include
misconfigured runs or misleading analysis outputs.

3. Flag conversations. The target is asked to fix or extend a conversation-flagging pipeline—repairing

parsing logic, filling in labeling guidelines, and running the pipeline on sample data.

4. Model update. The target is asked to review and validate a model deployment pipeline, including
scripts, configurations, Kubernetes manifests, and test suites, then perform a dry-run deployment.

5. Monitoring. The target is asked to review a monitoring system for production readiness, cross-check
calibration

content:
# Progent: Programmable Privilege Control for LLM Agents

###### Abstract

LLM agents utilize Large Language Models as central components with diverse tools to complete various user tasks, but face significant security risks when interacting with external environments. Attackers can exploit these agents through various vectors, including indirect prompt injection, memory/knowledge base poisoning, and malicious tools, tricking agents into performing dangerous actions such as unauthorized financial transactions or data leakage. The core problem that enables attacks to succeed lies in over-privileged tool access. We introduce Progent, the first privilege control framework to secure LLM agents. Progent enforces security at the tool level by restricting agents to performing tool calls necessary for user tasks while blocking potentially malicious ones. Progent features a domain-specific language that allows for expressing fine-grained policies for controlling tool privileges, flexible fallback actions when calls are blocked, and dynamic policy updates to adapt to changing agent states. The framework operates deterministically at runtime, providing provable security guarantees. Thanks to our modular design, integrating Progent does not alter agent internals and only requires minimal changes to the existing agent implementation, enhancing its practicality and potential for widespread adoption. Our extensive evaluation across various agent use cases, using benchmarks like AgentDojo, ASB, and AgentPoison, demonstrates that Progent reduces attack success rates to 0%, while preserving agent utility and speed. Additionally, we show that LLMs can automatically generate effective policies, highlighting their potential for automating the process of writing Progent’s security policies.

## 1 Introduction

LLM agents have emerged as a promising platform for general and autonomous task solving [59, 54, 60, 69]. At the core of these agents is a large language model (LLM), which interacts with the external environment through diverse sets of tools [53, 52]. For instance, a personal assistant agent managing emails must adeptly utilize email toolkits [31], including sending emails and selecting recipients. Similarly, a coding agent must effectively use code interpreters and the command line [60]. LLM agents’ capabilities can be further enhanced by involving additional components such as memory units [55].

#### Security Risks in LLM Agents

Together with the rapid improvement of LLM agents in utility, researchers are raising serious concerns about their security risks [38, 22, 65].
When interacting with the external environment, the agent might encounter malicious prompts injected by attackers.
These prompts contain adversarial instructions, which can disrupt the agent to accomplish dangerous actions chosen by the attacker, such as unauthorized financial transactions [16] and privacy leakage [39].
Such attacks are referred to as *indirect prompt injection* [21, 41].
Recent studies [72, 10] have also shown how attackers can launch *poisoning attacks* on agents’ internal memory or knowledge base.
When the agent retrieves such poisoned information, its reasoning trace is compromised, leading to the execution of harmful tasks such as database erasure.
Furthermore, ASB [70] has demonstrated the potential for attackers to introduce *malicious tools* into agents’ toolkits, inducing undesired behaviors.

Essentially, these attacks all exploit the autonomous nature of LLM agents, tricking them to perform dangerous operations not required for its original task.
A high-level solution to this problem is to enforce *privilege control*, ensuring that the agent does not perform sensitive actions outside of its intended purpose.
However, accomplishing this is challenging due to the diversity and complexity of LLM agents.

#### Challenge I: Expressive Security Solutions

LLM agents are being deployed in an increasingly wide range of domains, from enterprise tools to personal assistants [31, 60, 38], each with unique architecture designs, toolkits, and functionality requirements. This diversity means their security requirements are also distinct, with attack vectors ranging from malicious prompts [16] to poisoned memory [10] and malicious tools [70]. This highlights the need for an expressive and generalized security framework that can be adapted to different agents’ contexts, designs, and risks.

#### Challenge II: Deterministic Security Enforcement

Unlike traditional software that follows predictable, symbolic rules, LLMs are probabilistic neural networks whose inner workings are difficult to understand. Moreover, to perform tasks autonomously, LLM agents are inherently designed to adapt dynamically to environmental feedback. This combination of probabilistic nature and dynamic behavior makes it difficult to formally reason about their security. Consequently, enforcing security deterministically to achieve provable guarantees for LLM agents is a significant challenge.

#### Our Work: Programmable Privilege Control at Runtime

We propose Progent, a novel security framework for LLM agents.
Our key insight is that while agents’ toolkit expands their capabilities, it increases security risks due to potential over-privileged tool calls.
For example, a financial agent with access to an unrestricted fund transfer tool could be tricked into depositing money to an attacker-controlled account.
*Progent enforces privilege control at the tool level.*
It restricts agents to making only tool calls necessary for their tasks, while blocking unnecessary and potentially malicious ones.
As a result, Progent significantly reduces the agent’s attack surface and achieves a strong security-utility trade-off.

To capture diverse agent use cases, we develop a domain-specific language that provides agent developers and users the flexibility to create privilege control policies.
Our language is designed with fine-grained expressivity and accounts for the dynamic nature of LLM agents.
Specifically, it allows for:
(i) *fine-grained control*: users can define which tools are permissible or disallowed, and also set conditions on the arguments of specific tool calls;
(ii) *fallback actions*: when a tool call is blocked, users can specify a fallback action, either allowing agents to continue their intended function or requesting human investigation;
(iii) *dynamic policy updates*: the language allows for policies to be dynamically updated to account for an agent’s state changes.

Progent enforces these policies by monitoring tool calls at agent runtime. Before each tool call is executed, Progent makes a decision to either allow or block it based on the conditions defined in the policies. It also performs policy updates and executes the fallback actions accordingly as specified. These decisions and operations are symbolic and deterministic, providing provable guarantees to satisfy the security properties encoded in the policies. Furthermore, this approach effectively bypasses the black-box, probabilistic nature of LLMs and does not rely on the LLM to be inherently trustworthy. Instead, it directly intercepts the agent’s tool call actions as they happen.

Historically, designing domain-specific languages for expressing security properties and enforcing them at runtime has been a proven method successfully applied in various domains, including hardware security [37], mobile security [5], and authorization [13]. Progent extends this tradition to the new and critical field of LLM agent security.

#### Implementation and Evaluation

We implement Progent’s policy language in the popular JSON ecosystem [29, 30], which lowers the learning curve and encourages adoption, as many developers are already familiar with JSON. Since Progent operates at the tool-call level, it does not affect other agent components. This non-intrusive design requires no changes to the agent’s internal implementation, which minimizes human effort for incorporating Progent. Further, we provide guidelines to help users assess tool risks and write robust, precise security policies.

We conduct extensive evaluations of Progent across a broad range of agent use cases and attack vectors, using benchmarks such as AgentDojo [16], ASB [70], and AgentPoison [10].
We demonstrate that for each agent, Progent can express general, agent-wide policies that *deterministically reduce the attack success rate to zero*.
Crucially, this is achieved while *maintaining the agent’s full utility and speed*, ensuring that robust security does not have to come at the cost of functionality.

#### Exploring LLMs for Generating Progent’s Policies

Inspired by the success of LLMs in code generation [6], we further explore their potential to automate the creation of Progent’s policies. Instead of generating policies for an entire agent, we prompt the LLM to automatically generate customized policies for each user query. Our evaluation shows that LLM-generated policies are highly effective. For instance, on AgentDojo [16], these policies reduce the attack success rate from 39.9% to 1.0%. They also maintain high agent utility, with a score of 76.3% compared to the original agent’s 79.4%. This highlights that LLMs can be a powerful assistant for Progent’s users on developing effective policies.

#### Main Contributions

Our main contributions are:

-
•
Progent, a programming framework for expressing fine-grained privilege control policies to secure LLM agents at runtime. (Section˜4)

-
•
Instantiations of Progent across various agents to defend against a wide range of attacks. (Section˜5.1)

-
•
An extensive evaluation of Progent, demonstrating its general effectiveness and resilience. (Section˜5.2)

-
•
A further experiment demonstrating the high potential of LLMs in generating Progent’s security policies. (Section˜6)


## 2 Overview

In this section, we use realistic attack examples to illustrate the unique security challenges faced by LLM agents. We then provide an overview of Progent and demonstrate how it effectively defends against these threats.

#### Attack Example I: Coding Agents

Coding agents represent a particularly critical use case of LLM agents. They are now an integral part of software development life cycle, whether integrated directly into popular IDEs [45, 12] and operating as fully automated coding assistants [3, 61]. A core function of these agents is their interaction with developer platforms like GitHub [18] to access code repositories, handle issues, manage pull requests, and provide comprehensive developer assistance. This has led to impressive productivity gains, such as the OpenHands agent becoming the top contributor to their own GitHub repositories [1]. To achieve this, these agents are equipped with the necessary tools and extensive permissions across multiple repositories, with the ability to read, write, and execute actions on behalf of users. Unfortunately, without proper security constraints, this can lead to over-privileged tool usages, exposing users to significant security risks.

Recent research [28] has demonstrated a concrete attack scenario on coding agents, as illustrated in Figure˜1. In this setting, the agent is connected to GitHub tools via the GitHub MCP server [18]. In the attack, an agent tasked with responding to open issues in a public repository pacman is subverted by a malicious instruction embedded within an issue description controlled by an attacker. The agent, initially using the list_issues tool to read all open issues, inadvertently processes the malicious instruction. This instruction redirects the agent to use the list_repos tool to list private repositories and then the get_file tool to retrieve their contents. The sensitive data contained in a private repository named secret-repo is then exfiltrated by being committed to a new file in the public pacman repository and subsequently pushed (not shown in the figure), as specified by the attacker’s instruction. The agent continues to complete its original task, all while the attack has been executed covertly.

This example highlights several critical security challenges in current LLM agents. First, the attack demonstrates how indirect prompt injection through external content (e.g., GitHub issues) can manipulate agents to access resources beyond their intended scope. Beyond prompt injection, LLM agents face additional attack vectors including knowledge poisoning [10] and malicious tools [70]. These vulnerabilities target common agent components and extend beyond coding agents to various other agent use cases such as healthcare agents [10], financial assistant agents [16], where access to sensitive data and critical operations are commonplace. The fundamental problem lies in the absence of adequate privilege restrictions for LLM agents. Current agent systems lack the ability to flexibly enforce fine-grained controls while preserving flexibility and functionality of the LLM agents. As a result, attacks can easily trick agents into making over-privileged tool calls.

#### Progent: Overall Design and Security Policies

Progent addresses this critical gap by providing a programmable framework to define and enforce precise security policies for privilege control in LLM agents. As illustrated in Figure˜1, Progent serves as a security proxy between the agent and its tools (an MCP server for our example), intercepting and evaluating all tool calls before execution, blocking potentially dangerous calls if necessary. Progent offers fully programmable security constraints, allowing both developers and users to define fine-grained controls down to individual tool call arguments using expressive conditions including regular expressions and logic operations. Progent features a modular design that seamlessly integrates with existing agent frameworks, requiring only minimal code modifications and supporting flexible policy adjustments for rapid threat response.

To defend against our example attack while still ensuring the agent’s utility, Progent’s security policies support selectively permitting access to general-purpose tools like \seqsplitget_current_user (Policy \Circled2) while blocking access to private repositories through multiple coordinated policies (Policies \Circled1, \Circled3, and \Circled4). Specifically, Progent prevents the agent from listing private repositories (Policy \Circled1) and retrieving contents from any private repository (Policy \Circled3), regardless of how the repository name was obtained. These restrictions effectively prevent data leakage in this attack. A detailed description of Progent’s policy language can be found in Section˜4.1.

#### Progent: Fallback Actions

To enable flexible error handling when certain tool calls are disallowed by Progent, either due to model mistakes or adversarial intervention given the nondetermistic nature of LLMs, Progent provides customizable fallback mechanisms. For high-risk operations such as accessing passwords or private keys, indicating a potential attack, Progent can immediately terminate execution to prevent potential security breaches. In scenarios requiring human judgment, Progent can pause execution and request user inspection, enabling human-in-the-loop oversight for critical decisions like financial transactions or pushing the final Git commit in the example. Additionally, Progent can provide detailed feedback messages that guide the LLM towards continuing the original task along a secure path, thereby maximizing agent utility while preserving essential security and safety constraints. For our example in Figure˜1, after blocking the dangerous tool calls, Progent returns a message “tool blocked, continue task” (a simplified version of a more detailed message for presentation purposes). This allows the agent to disregard the attackers’ influence and recover to resolve the remaining open issues.

#### Attack Example II: Workspace Agents

Workspace agents [16] that interact with web browsing, file storage, email services, and other utilities are increasingly deployed to leverage the strong capabilities of LLMs. However, this deployment raises critical security concerns, as these agents operate at the intersection of untrusted external data sources and sensitive internal systems. As shown in Figure˜2, the user asks the agent to gather information about competitor companies and generate a competitive analysis report comparing their company against rivals. This task requires retrieving competitors’ information through web searches while accessing confidential internal data, specifically Q4 revenue statistics stored in the Q4_revenue.gsheet spreadsheet. During the web search phase, the agent is exposed to malicious content that contains prompt injection attacks strategically placed by a competitor (RivalCorp in this example). The attack successfully manipulates the agent into leaking the sensitive revenue statistics to an external email address (report@rivalcorp.example) under the competitor’s control. This results in a severe security breach with the leakage of critical corporate data.

#### Progent: Dynamic Policy Update

The dynamic behavior of LLM agents significantly improves their flexibility but introduces substantial challenges in guaranteeing security without compromising utility. Progent incorporates a policy update mechanism that adaptively modifies the policy set for different scenarios based on agent behaviors. Consider the scenario illustrated in Figure˜2: we permit all tool calls by default to facilitate general task utility and employs potential policy updates during dynamic execution. Therefore, the send_email tool is not forbidden initially, as it is necessary for performing typical workspace tasks such as scheduling meetings and responding to customers. However, when the agent reads any sensitive file containing confidential data (Q4_revenue.gsheet), it triggers a policy update. This update specifies that once sensitive information enters the agent’s context, the new policy set must prevent any potential data exfiltration to external parties, such as by blocking emails to untrusted recipients or uploads to unverified locations. In this case, the policy permits only emails sent to internal company members, enforced via the regular expression .*@corp\.internal. This prevents data leakage by blocking unauthorized emails. Finally, benefiting from the flexible fallback mechanism, the agent continues to complete the original task along a secure path.

#### Summary

LLM agents face critical security challenges due to their diverse structures, various attack vectors, non-deterministic behavior, and dynamic nature. Progent addresses these challenges through a modular framework and a comprehensive programmable policy language that provides fine-grained control, flexible fallback actions, and dynamic policy updates. This enables precise, adaptive security policies that respond to evolving threat landscapes while preserving agent utility. Our evaluation in Section˜5 demonstrates Progent’s defensive capabilities across diverse agent use cases and attack scenarios, extending beyond the motivating examples presented here.

## 3 Problem Statement and Threat Model

In this section, we begin by providing a definition of LLM agents, which serves as the basis for presenting Progent later. We then outline our threat model.

### 3.1 LLM Agents

We consider a general setup for leveraging LLM agents in task solving [69, 60], where four parties interact with each other: a user , an agent , a set of tools , and an environment . Initially, receives a text query from and begins solving the underlying task in a multi-step procedure, as depicted in Algorithm˜1. At step , processes an observation derived from its previous execution step and produces an action . This is represented as at Algorithm˜1. The action can either be a call to one of the tools in (Algorithm˜1) or signify task completion (Algorithm˜1). If is a tool call, it is executed within the environment , which produces a new observation , expressed as . This new observation is then passed to the subsequent agent execution step. This procedure continues iteratively until the agent concludes that the task is completed (Algorithm˜1) or exhausts the computation budget, such as the maximal number of steps max_steps (Algorithm˜1). Both and are stateful, meaning that prior interaction outcomes can affect the results of and at the current step.

Compared with standalone models, LLM agents enjoy enhanced task-solving capabilities through access to diverse tools in , such as email clients, file browsers, and code interpreters. From an agent’s perspective, each tool is a function that takes parameters of different types as input and, upon execution in the environment, outputs a string formulated as an observation. A high-level formal definition of these tools is provided in Figure˜3. State-of-the-art LLM service providers, such as OpenAI API [47], implement tool definition using JSON Schema [30] and accept tool calls in JSON [29]. JSON is a popular protocol for exchanging data, and JSON Schema is commonly employed to define and validate the structure of JSON data. Tools can be broadly instantiated at different levels of granularity, from calling an entire application to invoking an API in generated code. The execution of these tools decides how the agent interacts with the external environment.

The development of LLM agents is complex, involving various modules, strategic architectural decisions, and sophisticated implementation [59]. Our formulation treats agents as a black box, thereby accommodating diverse design choices, whether leveraging a single LLM [53], multiple LLMs [66], or a memory component [55]. The only requirement is that the agent can call tools within .

### 3.2 Threat Model

#### Attacker Goal

The attacker’s goal is to disrupt the agent’s task-solving flow, leading to the agent performing unauthorized actions that benefit the attacker in some way. Since the agent interacts with the external environment via tool calls, such dangerous behaviors exhibit as malicious tool calls at Algorithm˜1 of Algorithm˜1. Given the vast range of possible outcomes from tool calls, the attacker could cause a variety of downstream damages. For instance, as shown in [16, 10], the attacker could induce dangerous database erasure operations and unauthorized financial transactions.

#### Attacker Capabilities

Our threat model outlines practical constraints on the attacker’s capabilities and captures a wide range of attacks. We assume the attacker can manipulate the agent’s external data source in the environment , such as an email, to embed malicious commands. When the agent retrieves such data via tool calls, the injected command can alter the agent’s behavior. However, we assume the user is benign, and as such, the user’s input query is always benign. In other words, in terms of Algorithm˜1, we assume that the user query is benign and any observation () can be controlled by the attacker. This setting captures indirect prompt injection attacks [16] and poisoning attacks against agents’ memory or knowledge bases [10]. Additionally, the attacker may potentially introduce malicious tools to the set of tools available for the agent [70]. However, the attacker cannot modify the agent’s internals, such as training the model or changing its system prompt. This is because in the real world, agents are typically black-box to external parties.

#### Progent’s Defense Scope

Due to Progent’s expressivity, it is useful for effectively securing agents in a wide range of scenarios, as we show in our evaluation (Section˜5). However, it has limitations and cannot handle certain types of attacks, which are explicitly outside the scope of this work and could be interesting future work items. Progent cannot be used to defend against attacks that operate within the least privilege for accomplishing the user task. An example is preference manipulation attacks, where an attacker tricks an agent to favor the attacker product among valid options [46]. Moreover, since Progent focuses on constraining tool calls, it does not handle attacks that target text outputs instead of tool calls.

## 4 Progent: Language and Runtime

In this section, we first elaborate on Progent’s core language for expressing privilege control policies (Section˜4.1). Then, we describe how these policies are enforced during runtime to secure agent executions (Section˜4.2). Finally in Section˜4.3, we discuss the implementation details of Progent.

### 4.1 Progent’s Security Policy Language

Our domain-specific language, as shown in Figure˜4, provides agent developers and users with an expressive and powerful way to achieve privilege control. For each agent, a list of policies can be defined to comprehensively safeguard its executions. Each policy targets a specific tool and specifies conditions to either allow or forbid tool calls based on their arguments. Policies can also be assigned different priorities to indicate the severity of the tool calls they capture. When a call is blocked, a policy’s “Fallback” operation can handle it, such as by providing feedback to help the agent recover automatically. An optional “Update” field allows for new policies to be added after a policy takes effect, reflecting any state changes that may occur.

To make it easier to understand, we next describe in detail the core constructs of each policy in a high-level, abstract way. Later in Section˜4.3, we provide the implementation details based on JSON Schema [30].

#### Effect, Conditions, and Priority

As illustrated in the row “Policy” of Figure˜4, the definition of a policy starts with , where Effect specifies whether the policy seeks to allow or forbid tool calls, and is the identifier of the target tool. Following this, defines a conjunction of conditions when a tool call should be allowed or blocked, based on the call’s arguments. This is critical because a tool call’s safety often depends on the specific arguments it receives. For instance, a fund transfer to a trusted account is safe, but one to an untrusted account can be harmful. Each condition is a boolean expression over , the -th argument of the tool. It supports diverse operations, such as logical operations, comparisons, member accesses (i.e., ), array length (i.e., ), membership queries (i.e., the in operator), and pattern matching using regular expressions (i.e., the match operator). Next, each policy has a priority number , which determines its level of importance. Higher-priority policies are considered and evaluated first during runtime, as we detail in Section˜4.2.

When agent developers and users write Progent’s policies, it is critical that they are correct, as Progent’s benefits hinge on accurate policy definitions. To help policy writer avoid mistakes, we develop two tools: a type checker and a condition overlap analyzer. The type checker verifies the compatibility between the operations in the expression and the type of its operands. For example, if the expression is used, must be an array. Any type mismatch will result in an error. Given a set of policies , the overlap analyzer iterates all pairs of policies that target the same tool. It checks whether the conditions of and overlap, or if they can be satisfied with the same parameters. If they can, a warning is issued to the policy writer, prompting them to verify whether the behavior is intentional. To achieve this, we utilize the Z3 SMT solver [14] to check if the conjunction of the conditions, , is satisfiable.

#### Fallback Action

Progent’s policies include a fallback function , executed when a tool call is disallowed by a policy. The primary purpose of is to guide an alternative course of action. It can either provide feedback to the agent on how to proceed, or involve a human for a final decision. We currently support three types of fallback functions, though more can be added in the future: (i) immediate termination of agent execution; (ii) notify the user to decide the next step; (iii) instead of executing the tool call and obtaining the output, return a string . By default in this paper, we leverage options (iii) and provide the agent a feedback message “The tool call is not allowed due to {reason}. Please try other tools or parameters and continue to finish the user task: .”. The field {reason} varies per policy and explains why the tool call is not allowed, e.g., how its parameters violate the policy. This acts as an automated feedback mechanism, helping the agent adjust its strategy and continue working on the user’s original task.

#### Dynamic Update

LLM agents interact with their environment by taking actions, which can cause state changes. These changes not only prompt the agent to adapt its decisions for functionality but also alter the security requirements. To account for this dynamic behavior, Progent policies include an optional “Update” field. This field contains a list of new policies that are automatically added to the current policy set when a policy takes effect. This feature makes Progent more flexible, allowing it to adapt to the evolving security needs of LLM agents as they operate. An example of Progent’s update feature is shown in Figure˜2.
