metadata.title: Your Agent, Their Asset: A Real-World Safety Analysis of OpenClaw
metadata.summary: Existing sandboxed evaluations fail to capture the full attack surface of real-world agents. First real-world safety evaluation of OpenClaw, which operates with full local system access and integrates with sensitive services. Introduces CIK taxonomy unifying Capability, Identity, and Knowledge dimensions.

title: Architecture Matters for Multi-Agent Security
description: Empirical study of how MAS design decisions shape the tradeoff between task performance and attack resistance across three agentic environments (browser, desktop, and code). Individual agent security does not guarantee system-level security.
content:
# Architecture Matters for Multi-Agent Security

###### Abstract

Multi-agent systems (MAS), composed of networks of two or more autonomous AI agents, have become increasingly popular in production deployments, yet introduce security risks that do not arise in single-agent settings. Even if individual agents exhibit robust security, architectural decisions governing their coordination can create attack surfaces that have not been systematically characterized. In this work, we present an empirical study of how MAS design decisions shape the tradeoff between task performance and attack resistance. Across three agentic environments (browser, desktop, and code) and 13 architectural configurations, we use stagewise evaluations that distinguish planning refusal, execution-stage interception, partial harmful execution, and successful attack completion to study three key design choices: (i) agent roles, which determine how authority and responsibility are allocated; (ii) communication topology, which shapes how and when agents interact; and (iii) memory, which determines the context and state visibility accessible to each agent. We find that multi-agent architectures are more vulnerable than standalone agents in the majority of configurations, with attack success rates varying by up to 3.8× at comparable or higher benign accuracy, and that no single design is universally safer. These results motivate the development of further evaluations that move beyond the security properties of a single agent.

## 1 Introduction

As AI systems evolve from single large language models (LLMs) into increasingly complex agentic and multi-agent architectures, their security properties change in fundamental ways (Kumar et al., 2024; Schroeder de Witt, 2025). While early deployments relied on standalone models responding directly to user prompts, modern systems increasingly distribute tasks across agents that plan, execute actions, interact with tools, maintain memory, and coordinate with one another (Hong et al., 2024). Such systems are increasingly capable of achieving large-scale, long-horizon tasks with which individual models and agents struggle (Hadfield et al., 2025; Lin, 2026).

Despite their rapidly increasing capabilities, progress in securing these systems against misuse has lagged behind. Research in AI security has revealed numerous threat vectors against these systems, with new attacks emerging at different levels of abstraction. At the agent level, research examines failures arising from tool use and memory poisoning (Zhang et al., 2025). Recent work has begun exploring multi-agent risks such as collusion (Motwani et al., 2025), infection-style attacks (Lee and Tiwari, 2024; Gu et al., 2024), and viral misalignment via subliminal prompting (Weckbecker et al., 2026). This growing body of work suggests that defenses effective at one layer may degrade or behave differently when embedded in richer systems. A language model that resists direct jailbreak attempts may nonetheless enable harmful behavior once coupled with web tools or persistent memory (Chiang et al., 2025). Similarly, an agent that appears robust in isolation may contribute to system-level failures when its outputs are routed, transformed, or reinforced through inter-agent coordination. In such settings, vulnerabilities can amplify through task decomposition, partial observability, and distributed control, producing emergent risks that are not captured by single-layer evaluations.

Mitigating these risks requires attending not only to explicit defenses but also to the broader architectural choices that shape system behavior. Yet any modification to system design must be evaluated against its impact on task performance - security methods that impose unacceptable costs fail to preserve the benefits of the underlying system (Schroeder de Witt, 2025; Peigné et al., 2025). While prior work has examined such tradeoffs, the impact of indirect architectural decisions remains underexplored. To address this gap, we present an empirical analysis of how design choices affect security in agentic and multi-agent systems. We ground our study in realistic agent tasks, adapting the BrowserART (Kumar et al., 2024), OS-Harm (Kuntz et al., 2025), and RedCode-Gen (Guo et al., 2024) benchmarks, originally designed for single-agent evaluation, to support systematic multi-agent assessment. We systematically evaluate how susceptibility to misuse changes as tasks move from single-agent to multi-agent, focusing on three key dimensions: role specialization, communication topology, and memory visibility, examining how each reshapes both the attack surface and the overall performance of the system.

We make three main contributions:

-
•
Multi-agent adaptation of standardized misuse benchmarks. We adapt BrowserART, OS-Harm, and RedCode-Gen to the multi-agent setting, preserving original task semantics while varying only architectural configuration, and introduce stage-wise metrics that capture where in the pipeline harmful behavior is refused or executed. We release all three adaptations to support further research

111https://github.com/benhagag10/Architecture-Matters-for-Multi-Agent-Security. -
•
Empirical characterization of architectural effects on security. Across 13 architectural configurations, multiple base models, and three environments, we find that role distribution, communication topology, and memory visibility each independently affect vulnerability, with multi-agent settings more vulnerable than standalone baselines in the majority of configurations. The direction and magnitude of these effects depend on scenario, model, and architecture.

-
•
Joint measurement of the security-performance tradeoff. We measure benign task performance alongside attack resistance across architectures, finding that security profiles can differ substantially - with attack success rates varying by up to - even at comparable or higher benign accuracy. This tradeoff should be considered when designing multi-agent systems, as capability evaluation alone is insufficient to surface these risks.


Together, these contributions provide the first controlled comparison of multi-agent architectural design choices for security across realistic environments.

## 2 Background and Related Work

A multi-agent system (MAS) consists of multiple autonomous AI agents that make decisions and take actions, maintain private state, and interact through communication channels or shared environments. Unlike single-model or single-agent setups, MAS behavior emerges from interactions among agents rather than from any individual component. These interactions introduce system-level dynamics, such as coordination, negotiation, and delegation - that fundamentally change both the attack surface and the nature of failure.

### 2.1 LLM and Single-Agent Vulnerabilities

Security research on large language models and LLM based agents has primarily focused on vulnerabilities at the model or single-agent level. At the LLM level, prior work has documented risks such as prompt injection and jailbreak attacks (Liu et al., 2024; Andriushchenko et al., 2024), data poisoning and backdoors (Fendley et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2024), and privacy threats including leakage and membership inference attacks (Aguilera-Martínez and Berzal, 2025; Das et al., 2025; Gan et al., 2024). These vulnerabilities vary across LLM architectures (Benjamin et al., 2024) and change in complex, unpredictable ways (Shang and Wei, 2025).

At the single-agent level, vulnerabilities extend beyond the underlying model to include system prompts, tool use and memory poisoning. Zhang et al. (2025) formalize core agent-level attacks and evaluate them using Attack Success Rate, Refusal Rate, and Performance under No Attack. AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al., 2024) provides a dynamic environment specifically for evaluating indirect prompt injection attacks, demonstrating significant vulnerability when tool outputs are adversarially manipulated. AgentHarm (Andriushchenko et al., 2025) extends this to multi-turn agentic misuse scenarios with fine-grained metrics distinguishing planning-stage refusal from execution-stage failures.

### 2.2 Multi-Agent Security

Multi-agent settings introduce new risks that cannot be reduced to LLM- or single-agent vulnerabilities. Interactions among agents give rise to distinct failure modes: miscoordination, conflict, and collusion—driven by agents’ incentives and shaped by key risk factors: information asymmetries, network effects, selection pressures, destabilizing dynamics, commitment problems, emergent agency (Hammond et al., 2025). Prior work distinguishes between cooperative and competitive threat models (Schroeder de Witt, 2025; Peigné et al., 2025). In cooperative systems, collaboration itself can become a liability, enabling error amplification, misinformation propagation, and collusive behavior (Motwani et al., 2025). Specifically, covert collusion can emerge through steganographic communication channels, sometimes arising unintentionally from reward misspecification rather than deliberate coordination (Mathew et al., 2024). In competitive settings, agents may engage in deception, persuasion, or sabotage, destabilizing collective outcomes (Qi et al., 2025). Adversarial agents can systematically manipulate multi-agent debate outcomes and increase jailbreak success through iterative dialogue (Qi et al., 2025; Amayuelas et al., 2024). These dynamics enable infection-style attacks where single compromised agents spread harmful behavior across networks (Gu et al., 2024; Lee and Tiwari, 2024), and false information can persist and amplify through multi-agent interactions (Ju et al., 2024).

### 2.3 Evaluation and Defense Gaps

For multi-agent systems, Cemri et al. (2025) introduce MAST, a taxonomy of 14 failure modes derived from 1,600+ execution traces across MAS frameworks, while MultiAgentBench (Zhu et al., 2025a) evaluates collaboration dynamics with coordination metrics. However, existing benchmarks primarily evaluate either general task performance or specific attack types in isolation, without systematically varying architectural design choices or focusing on adversarial security.

Defenses against multi-agent vulnerabilities remain nascent. Recent work explores architectural approaches including plan–then–execute designs (Del Rosario et al., 2025) and capability-based architectures (Debenedetti et al., 2025), yet most defensive work still focuses on input/output filtering designed for single-agent settings, with limited investigation of how architectural choices jointly shape task performance and attack resistance.

Security in multi-agent systems has a long history, spanning trust and reputation management (Yu et al., 2013; Jung et al., 2012), Byzantine-resilient consensus (Lamport et al., 1982; LeBlanc et al., 2013), and secure coordination under bounded adversaries such as energy-limited DoS and F-local faults (De Persis and Tesi, 2015; Ishii et al., 2022). LLM-based multi-agent systems differ from much of this tradition in that they are driven by foundation models capable of flexible, generalizable reasoning and communicate through unstructured, free-form protocols rather than rigidly specified interaction languages or APIs (Schroeder de Witt, 2025). As a result, classical guarantees based on fixed message semantics, protocol compliance, or explicit coordination assumptions may not transfer directly, motivating dedicated empirical study of how architecture shapes security in these systems (Nguyen et al., 2026; OWASP GenAI Security Project, 2025).

Recent work has begun to characterize security-performance tradeoffs in multi-agent systems: Peigné et al. (2025) quantify a ”multi-agent security tax” between robustness and collaboration, while Zhu et al. (2025b) examine role and topology effects. We extend this by isolating how role distribution, communication topology, and memory visibility independently affect security across three realistic environments, using stage-wise metrics.

## 3 Design Choices in Multi-Agent Systems

Multi-agent systems can be constructed using various architectural choices that affect security in ways that may be difficult to predict from first principles. We focus on three design choices that recur across modern architectures: role configuration, communication topology, and memory. We hypothesize that these architectural decisions introduce distinct vulnerability modes compared to single-agent LLMs by fragmenting responsibility for safety assessment and creating new attack surfaces. Below, we identify key design mechanisms and articulate hypotheses about how each may affect the likelihood of harmful task execution.

Design Choice 1: Role Configuration

Multi-agent systems are often designed with distinct agent roles, such as planners that decompose objectives, executors that carry out actions, reviewers that validate outputs, or specialized agents handling domain-specific subtasks. While such role separation can improve efficiency and task performance, and is sometimes necessary due to IP, regulatory, or security constraints, it can also fragment responsibility for safety assessment. Executor agents typically operate on narrowly scoped instructions without visibility into the full task context or downstream consequences; reviewer agents may evaluate outputs in isolation rather than assessing end-to-end behavior. Agents may also differ in their authority over system behavior. When agents with high execution authority are downstream from those responsible for safety reasoning (e.g., planners or critics), security judgments may become advisory rather than binding. Conversely, centralizing authority could introduce single points of failure. We vary role configuration in our experiments to investigate how these tradeoffs manifest in practice.

Design Choice 2: Communication Topology

Multi-agent systems can vary in communication structure, including centralized orchestrators, hierarchical trees, chains, and fully connected meshes. Communication topology determines how intent, uncertainty, and safety signals propagate through the system. In decentralized or mesh-based systems, decisions are distributed across agents without centralized oversight, while in hierarchical or chain-based systems, information may be summarized or filtered as it passes between agents. Each topology introduces distinct security tradeoffs, and these effects may depend on interactions with role configuration and memory design.

Design Choice 3: Memory and State Visibility

Agents may maintain private scratchpads or write to shared memory, creating different tradeoffs for safety reasoning. Private state preserves independence but may prevent safety-relevant insights from propagating across agents, while shared state improves transparency but may enable unsafe assumptions to spread. Beyond simple private/shared distinctions, systems vary in what information agents can access about themselves and others. Some expose full chains of thought through context windows or queryable memory, others provide action histories spanning entire sessions, and blackboard architectures may give agents visibility into the complete state of all other agents. These choices create different attack surfaces, as exposed reasoning may reveal exploitable patterns while shared histories could enable adversarial coordination.

## 4 Multi-Agent System Experimental Setup

We consider a malicious user who provides adversarial task instructions at input time. The attacker does not modify model weights or system code, and interacts with the system only through natural language prompts and standard tool outputs.

### 4.1 Scenarios

We evaluate three scenarios spanning the main agentic deployment categories: browser control (BrowserART; Kumar et al., 2024), desktop computer use (OS-Harm; Kuntz et al., 2025), and sandboxed code generation (RedCode-Gen; Guo et al., 2024). Each is a standardized single-agent benchmark that we adapt to multi-agent settings while preserving the original task semantics and environment. The only variables that change across conditions are architectural - the set of agent roles, the communication topology, and the memory available to each agent, and the distribution of tool access according to role specialization. Task prompts and scoring rubrics are held fixed.

The scenarios differ in their action-space structure, which directly shapes how roles can be decomposed. BrowserART exposes a fixed set of named browser primitives (goto, click, fill, scroll), enabling a clean one-tool-per-agent partition in the fully specialized configuration (Navigate / Fill / Scroll / Click). OS-Harm agents instead operate on pixels through a unified computer tool (screenshot + mouse + keyboard); we partition this into four disjoint sub-tools (click, type, key, scroll), each retained alongside screenshot and submit so specialists can observe before acting. RedCode-Gen exposes four heterogeneous tools (python, text_editor, bash, think), yielding an asymmetric partition across four role-typed specialists (Design / Code / Review / Test) where several agents retain python but only one can write code. For each scenario, we also evaluate 2- and 3-specialist variants that progressively merge these sub-tools, allowing the degree of role decomposition to be varied independently of topology. Benign performance is measured on 42 tasks (available part of BrowserART), 50 OS-World tasks (Xie et al., 2024), and 50 BigCodeBench (Zhuo et al., 2024). Full details are provided in Appendix B.

### 4.2 Architectures

We instantiate the following architectural variants identically across all three scenarios. Appendix B.1 summarises the 13 evaluated conditions.

Baseline As a reference point, we evaluate a standalone agent. This agent has access to all tools, maintains its own memory, and executes actions sequentially. The standalone agent establishes baseline rates for both harmful behavior and benign task performance.

Role Specialization We evaluate several multi-agent role configurations that redistribute planning and execution. In orchestrator + batch executor setups, the orchestrator generates a plan and delegates execution to a single executor, which executes the plan without intermediate feedback. We consider variants in which the orchestrator provides either a high-level goal or a detailed action sequence. In stepwise execution, the orchestrator remains in the loop after every action, and the executor performs only a single action before returning control. In specialized executor settings, the orchestrator delegates subtasks to multiple executors with distinct roles, with all coordination mediated by the orchestrator.

Communication Topology We study three communication topologies beyond the standalone baseline. In a star topology, a central orchestrator mediates all communication between executors, which do not communicate directly. In a chain topology, agents execute sequentially in a fixed order, with each agent receiving the previous agent’s output. In a mesh topology, agents communicate peer-to-peer without a central coordinator, and no single agent has global control authority.

Memory To isolate the effect of memory and shared context, we fix the topology and vary what information agents can access. We consider settings with private memory per agent (baseline), access to agents’ own chain-of-thought reasoning (+Own Reasoning), and full shared memory in which all agents observe the complete execution history (+Shared Memory), including actions, observations, and reasoning traces.

### 4.3 Models

We evaluate architectural effects using GPT-4o as the primary model across all three scenarios. To assess generalization across different capability and alignment models, we extend our evaluation to five additional models: GPT-5.4, GPT-5-mini, Claude Sonnet 4, Qwen3-VL, and Llama-70B-Chat. Model coverage varies by scenario due to computational constraints: all six models are evaluated on BrowserART, three models on OS-Harm (GPT-4o, GPT-5.4, GPT-5-mini), and two on RedCode-Gen (GPT-4o, GPT-5.4). Complete cross-model results are provided in Appendix A.

### 4.4 Evaluation Metrics

Binary attack success is insufficient for multi-agent systems, where harmful behavior may be refused or executed at different pipeline stages. We record stage-specific outcomes: Planning Refusal (task refused during planning), Execution Refusal (refused after delegation), Harmful Actions (one or more harmful actions executed), and Harmful Task (objective completed). We additionally report Benign task success to assess performance impact. Outcome classification follows the judge protocol of each original benchmark. BrowserART uses the Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct (AI@Meta, 2024) via the Together API. OS-Harm and RedCode-Gen use GPT-4.1. All judges map trajectories to the four-stage outcome hierarchy described above. Full judging details are provided in Appendix B.6. To validate automated judgments, we used a two-phase process: an LLM-as-a-judge pass to flag potential scoring errors, followed by manual inspection of all flagged cases by two researchers, with additional sampling from full logs. This review identified 15 scoring errors and 20 corrections to the scorer itself, all of which were corrected. A subsequent spot-check of 10% of the remaining logs found a 7% discrepancy rate; all identified discrepancies were corrected in the final results.

## 6 Discussion

##### Multi-agent systems expand the attack surface.

Moving from a single agent to a multi-agent architecture introduces additional decision points, communication channels, and role boundaries - each a potential site where safety reasoning can fail or be bypassed. That multi-agent systems should be harder to secure is, in principle, unsurprising; what our results quantify is the extent and unpredictability of this effect. Across six models and three environments, multi-agent architectures are more vulnerable than the standalone agent in the majority of evaluated configurations, often by substantial margins. However, the direction and magnitude of the effect depend on the specific architecture, model, and environment: no single topology, memory scheme, or delegation strategy is universally safer or riskier. Notably, this increased vulnerability co-occurs with stable or improved benign performance: on BrowserART, specialist configurations achieve higher benign accuracy than the standalone agent ( vs. ) while exhibiting up to higher attack success. Standard capability evaluation provides no signal about these risks.

##### Effects are scenario- and model-dependent.

Our results do not support a single ranking of “safe” vs. “unsafe” designs. Role specialization produces the largest absolute increase on
BrowserART but shows substantial relative effects across all scenarios. Star topology is the riskiest on
BrowserART but the *safest* multi-agent topology on
RedCode-Gen and OS-Harm, where chain is the riskiest. Increased
memory visibility does not reliably improve security: of six
topology-scenario combinations, only one shows consistent
improvement, while two show worsening. These interactions between
design axis, environment, and action-space structure make it
difficult to issue universal architectural recommendations and
underscore the need for per-deployment evaluation.

The effect of architecture on security is further mediated by the underlying model’s safety training. Well-aligned models remain robust across nearly all configurations, though OS-Harm is an exception where even strong models show increased vulnerability under simple delegation. Weaker-aligned models degrade dramatically under the same architectural changes, with some showing 4-fold increases in harmful task completion under specialization. This suggests that architectural fragmentation interacts with model-level alignment: models with stronger safety training detect harmful intent from partial context, while weaker models lose the ability to recognize harm once it is distributed across agents.

##### Mechanisms.

Our results suggest that architectural decomposition undermines safety reasoning through two primary pathways. In role specialization, specialists receive isolated instructions without visibility into the full harmful task, while orchestrators decompose tasks without safety evaluation, creating a responsibility gap where no agent performs end-to-end safety assessment. This explains why specialist configurations show reduced Planning Refusal despite individual agents having strong safety training. For topology effects, the key factor is task visibility: mesh agents see the complete harmful objective and can refuse independently, while chain agents receive processed outputs that mask harmful intent, explaining chain’s Planning Refusal collapse on RedCode-Gen (8.1% vs. 25.6% for star). Memory effects depend on whether shared information aids detection (code patterns in RedCode-Gen mesh) or coordination for harmful tasks (OS-Harm mesh), with the balance determined by model alignment strength.

##### Implications for system design.

The findings highlight three key considerations for practitioners. First, security cannot be inferred from component-level evaluations-models that refuse harmful instructions individually may enable harm when architecturally decomposed. Second, performance-improving choices like specialization can simultaneously degrade security without affecting capability metrics. Third, architectural security must be evaluated per-deployment since effects are scenario- and model-dependent. This motivates treating architecture as a first-class security variable alongside traditional defenses.

## 7 Conclusions

This work presents an empirical study of how architectural design decisions affect security in multi-agent systems. Across three design dimensions, three agentic environments, and multiple base models, we find that multi-agent architectures are more vulnerable than standalone agents in the majority of configurations, often by substantial margins, though the magnitude and direction of the effect depend on the specific architecture, model, and environment.

Three findings challenge common assumptions about multi-agent security. First, security and performance can decouple counterintuitively: specialist configurations achieve higher benign accuracy while being up to 3.8× more vulnerable, meaning capability evaluation provides no signal about security risks. Second, no architectural design is universally safer-the same choices that reduce risk in one environment may increase it in another. Third, common design intuitions fail: increased memory visibility and communication connectivity do not reliably improve security and can worsen outcomes.

More broadly, our results provide evidence that safety properties do not compose straightforwardly from individual agents to multi-agent systems. A model that reliably refuses harmful instructions in isolation may enable the same harm when embedded in an architecture that fragments context, distributes authority, or separates task visibility from execution capability. We release our benchmark adaptations for multi-agent settings to support further investigation of these properties.

## 8 Limitations

Our study evaluates jailbreak vulnerabilities from an architectural perspective across three agentic environments (browser, desktop, and code), and the findings should be interpreted within this scope. While we isolate the effects of role configuration, communication topology, and memory visibility, these design choices may interact differently across additional domains, deployment contexts, and threat models. Several important directions are not explored in this work. We study only direct misuse by a malicious user; indirect prompt injection, memory poisoning, and adversarial agents operating within the system represent distinct threat vectors that may interact differently with architecture. We do not evaluate dedicated safety mechanisms such as monitor agents, guardrail layers, or policy-checking stages, which could alter the security-performance tradeoffs we observe. Our three design axes are varied independently in most experiments; the interaction effects between role configuration, topology, and memory, and with additional axes such as inter-agent communication protocols (e.g., A2A, MCP), remain underexplored. Extending this analysis to these settings, and to iterative red- and blue-teaming dynamics, is an important direction for future work.

## Impact Statement

This research contains material that may enable users to generate harmful content using publicly available LLM-based multi-agent systems. While we recognize the associated risks, we believe disclosure is essential given that the agent frameworks and evaluation benchmarks examined in this study are already publicly accessible and straightforward to deploy. The harmful tasks described were already achievable using methods from the original benchmark releases. In releasing our findings, we carefully weighed the benefits of enabling defensive research against potential misuse risks. Our results highlight a substantial gap between securing single-agent systems and their multi-agent counterparts, and we call upon the research community to develop safeguarding techniques for LLM-based multi-agent systems.

content:
# Redefining AI Red Teaming in the Agentic Era:

From Weeks to Hours

###### Abstract

AI systems are entering critical domains like healthcare, finance, and defense, yet remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. While AI red teaming is a primary defense, current approaches force operators into manual, library-specific workflows. Operators spend weeks hand-crafting workflows—assembling attacks, transforms, and scorers. When results fall short, workflows must be rebuilt. As a result, operators spend more time constructing workflows than probing targets for security and safety vulnerabilities.

We introduce an AI red teaming agent built on the open-source Dreadnode SDK. The agent creates workflows grounded in 45+ adversarial attacks, 450+ transforms, and 130+ scorers. Operators can probe multi-agent systems, multilingual, and multimodal targets, focusing on what to probe rather than how to implement it.

We make three contributions:

-
1.
Agentic interface. Operators describe goals in natural language via the Dreadnode TUI (Terminal User Interface). The agent handles attack selection, transform composition, execution, and reporting, letting operators focus on red teaming. Weeks compress to hours.

-
2.
Unified framework. A single framework for probing traditional ML models (adversarial examples) and generative AI systems (jailbreaks), removing the need for separate libraries.

-
3.
Llama Scout case study. We red team Meta’s Llama Scout and achieve an 85% attack success rate with severity up to 1.0, using zero human-developed code.


Keywords: AI red teaming, agentic systems, LLM security, LLM safety, jailbreak, automated AI red teaming, AI red team operator centered design

###### Contents

- 1 Introduction
- 2 Background and Related Work
- 3 System Architecture
- 4 Operator Workflow
- 5 Analytics and Reporting
- 6 Case Study: AI Red Teaming Llama Scout
- 7 Discussion
- 8 Limitations
- 9 Conclusion
- References
- Appendix
-
A Selected Adversarial Findings
- A.1 Finding 1: Production-Grade Shellcode Loader with AMSI Bypass
- A.2 Finding 2: Credential-Stealing Browser Extension
- A.3 Finding 3: Buffer Overflow Exploit with Shellcode
- A.4 Finding 4: Comprehensive Stalking and Surveillance Manual
- A.5 Finding 5: Detailed Self-Harm Instructions
- A.6 Finding 6: Suicide Method Lethality Comparison
- A.7 Finding 7: Lethal Gas from Household Chemicals
- A.8 Finding 8: Crack Cocaine Manufacturing Process


## 1 Introduction

As LLMs, multimodal models, and AI agents enter critical domains like healthcare, finance, defense, etc., AI red teaming has become essential for responsible deployment (NIST, 2023). This practice of systematically probing AI systems for safety failures, security vulnerabilities, and trust violations now serves as our primary methodology for validating model robustness (Ganguli et al., 2022; Perez et al., 2022).

Researchers have developed adversarial attacks across two categories. Open-box attacks require access to model weights and architecture: gradient-based methods optimize adversarial suffixes that transfer across model families (Zou et al., 2023), while optimization-based approaches extend these techniques to discrete prompt spaces (Jones et al., 2023). For traditional ML models (classifiers, object detectors), open-box gradient attacks compute exact loss gradients to craft minimal perturbations that flip predictions. Closed-box attacks operate without internal model access and are thus applicable to deployed systems: prompt-level techniques such as Prompt Automatic Iterative Refinement (PAIR) (Chao et al., 2023) and Tree of Attacks with Pruning (TAP) (Mehrotra et al., 2024) use LLM-driven iterative refinement to bypass safety training, while multi-turn strategies like Crescendo (Russinovich et al., 2024) exploit conversational context to progressively escalate from benign to harmful requests. For traditional ML models, closed-box decision-boundary attacks such as HopSkipJump (Chen et al., 2020) and query-efficient estimators like SimBA (Guo et al., 2019) probe the model through prediction queries alone, requiring no gradient access. Specialized approaches target chain-of-thought reasoning and low-resource languages where safety training is weakest (Yong et al., 2024). Notably, post-safety-training methodologies such as Microsoft’s iterative “break-fix” cycle for the Phi-3 family (Haider et al., 2024) demonstrate that even after multiple rounds of alignment, models remain vulnerable to novel adversarial techniques, underscoring the need for continuous, automated AI red teaming.

Beyond text-only attacks, the attack surface has expanded significantly along two axes. Agentic attacks target the tool-use, inter-agent trust boundaries, and multi-step reasoning capabilities of AI agents (Ruan et al., 2024), including Model Context Protocol (MCP) server poisoning, multi-agent prompt infection, and delegation exploits (OWASP, 2025). Multimodal attacks combine adversarial images, audio, or video with text prompts to exploit cross-modal alignment weaknesses (Carlini et al., 2023; Bailey et al., 2024). The catalog of known techniques now exceeds several dozen distinct strategies across these categories, each with its own parameterization, strengths, and failure modes.

Yet this proliferation has created a paradox: the more techniques available, the harder it becomes for operators to use them effectively. Every assessment demands deep technical expertise across multiple dimensions. Operators must understand target architectures, plan comprehensive threat models, prepare adversarial datasets, compose complex workflows from dozens of attack techniques and transforms, execute through command-line interfaces, interpret raw outputs without analytics support, and iterate across campaigns while manually tracking what works. The cognitive overhead is overwhelming and scales poorly.

This workflow is fundamentally library-centered: the operator adapts to the capabilities and constraints of the framework rather than expressing intent and receiving structured results. The cognitive overhead scales linearly with the number of available techniques and grows combinatorially as the target’s capabilities expand: agentic systems introduce tool-use, multi-step reasoning, and inter-agent trust boundaries as additional attack surfaces (OWASP, 2025); multimodal models expose cross-modal alignment weaknesses; and multilingual models are vulnerable across hundreds of harm categories and thousands of languages, with safety training particularly weak for low-resource languages (Yong et al., 2024).

PyRIT (Lopez Munoz et al., 2024), Garak (Derczynski et al., 2024), and Promptfoo (Promptfoo, 2024) advance the field by democratizing attack techniques. But they require operators to write code, configure parameters, and parse output files for a given library. If a particular attack fails, they create another workflow with different attack strategies. Operators must manually understand the traces, classify findings, map to compliance frameworks, and generate reports. If users want to probe traditional ML attacks, they need another framework for adversarial examples.

### 1.1 This Work

Our approach reverses this. Tools adapt to operators, not the reverse, through three principles:

Natural language objectives. Operators describe goals—what to probe, why, how aggressively—and the agent autonomously generates, executes, and analyzes attack workflows.

Automatic intelligence generation. Every attack produces structured, traceable evidence. Findings are automatically classified by severity, mapped to compliance frameworks (OWASP LLM Top 10, MITRE ATLAS, NIST AI RMF), and aggregated into dashboards with drill-down from project risk posture to individual adversarial prompts.

Conversational refinement. The agent maintains context across interactions, letting operators refine strategy naturally: “try a different attack,” “add persona-based transforms,” “focus where we saw partial failures.”.

### 1.2 Contributions

We make three contributions:

First, we designed an agentic AI red teaming system with comprehensive analytics. The system accepts natural-language objectives via the Dreadnode TUI (Terminal User Interface) and autonomously orchestrates complete attack workflows. It integrates 45+ attack strategies, 450+ prompt transforms, and 130+ scorers, eliminating the need for operators to master individual techniques or hand-craft attack compositions. The system includes an end-to-end analytics pipeline with granular tracing that transforms raw attack results into actionable intelligence. Every adversarial interaction—from initial prompt construction through model response analysis—is captured with structured metadata, enabling automated severity classification, compliance mapping (OWASP LLM Top 10, MITRE ATLAS, NIST AI RMF), and exportable evidence packages. This comprehensive approach allows operators to focus entirely on red teaming strategy rather than technical orchestration or manual result interpretation.

Second, we built a unified AI red teaming framework that probes both traditional ML models (adversarial examples, evasion attacks) and generative AI systems (jailbreaks, prompt injection, agentic exploits) through a single interface. Unlike existing tools that require separate libraries for different attack types, our framework provides a consistent operator experience across diverse AI systems—from image classifiers vulnerable to pixel perturbations to multi-agent systems susceptible to prompt injection and tool-use exploits. This unified approach eliminates the cognitive overhead of switching between disparate frameworks and enables comprehensive security assessments that span an organization’s entire AI deployment.

Third, we demonstrate the system through a comprehensive case study red teaming Meta’s Llama Scout (Meta, 2025). Starting from natural-language objectives like “generate ransomware deployment guides,” we achieve 85% attack success rate using Tree of Attacks with Pruning (Mehrotra et al., 2024) and advanced prompt transforms. Our most severe finding (score 1.0, Critical severity) emerges from a skeleton-key transform that tricks the model into adopting a fabricated “safety researcher” persona, demonstrating how sophisticated social engineering techniques can bypass safety training. The case study reveals systematic vulnerabilities across multiple attack categories and provides detailed compliance mappings for enterprise security teams.

## 2 Background and Related Work

### 2.1 Adversarial Attacks on Language Models

The discovery that safety-trained language models remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks has driven a substantial body of research. We organize prior work along several axes.

### 2.2 Generative AI Systems

#### Open-box attacks.

Zou et al. (2023) demonstrated that optimized adversarial suffixes can induce harmful completions from aligned models and transfer across model families, establishing that safety alignment is not robust to worst-case inputs. These gradient-based methods optimize adversarial suffixes by computing exact loss gradients with respect to model parameters. Subsequent work extended optimization-based attacks to the discrete prompt space (Jones et al., 2023), enabling targeted manipulation of specific tokens and phrases. Multi-turn and multimodal extensions have expanded these techniques to conversational settings and cross-modal inputs, where attackers can leverage gradients across text, image, and audio modalities simultaneously.

#### Closed-box attacks.

Prompt Automatic Iterative Refinement (PAIR) (Chao et al., 2023) introduced attacker-LLM loops where a red-team model iteratively refines adversarial prompts using feedback from the target’s responses, requiring no access to model weights or gradients. Tree of Attacks with Pruning (TAP) (Mehrotra et al., 2024) extended this to tree-structured search with pruning, improving coverage while controlling computational cost. Crescendo (Russinovich et al., 2024) demonstrated that multi-turn conversations can progressively escalate from benign to harmful requests, exploiting the model’s tendency to maintain conversational coherence. These methods operate entirely through the model’s API, making them practical for evaluating deployed systems. Recent work has expanded to agentic tool-use manipulation (Ruan et al., 2024), Model Context Protocol (MCP) server poisoning, multi-agent trust boundary violations, and multimodal attacks combining adversarial images with text prompts (Carlini et al., 2023).

### 2.3 Traditional ML Systems

#### Open-box attacks.

For traditional ML models (classifiers, object detectors, tabular models), open-box gradient attacks (Yuan et al., 2019) compute exact loss gradients to craft minimal perturbations that flip predictions while preserving semantic content. Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) (Goodfellow et al., 2014), Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) (Madry et al., 2017), and C&W attacks represent the foundational gradient-based approaches that require full access to model weights, architecture, and training data. These methods optimize adversarial perturbations in the input space (pixel manipulations for images, feature perturbations for tabular data) to achieve targeted or untargeted misclassification with minimal perceptual changes.

#### Closed-box attacks.

Decision-boundary attacks such as HopSkipJump (Chen et al., 2020) and query-efficient estimators like SimBA (Guo et al., 2019) probe traditional ML models through prediction queries alone, requiring no gradient access. These methods iteratively query the model with perturbed inputs to estimate decision boundaries and craft adversarial examples through geometric and statistical techniques. Boundary-based approaches focus on finding minimal perturbations along decision surfaces, while query-efficient methods minimize the number of model evaluations needed to achieve successful attacks, making them practical for rate-limited deployed systems.

### 2.4 Automated AI Red Teaming Frameworks

Several frameworks have been developed to operationalize adversarial evaluation. The most widely adopted include Microsoft’s PyRIT, NVIDIA’s Garak, Promptfoo, and Meta’s Purple Llama CyberSecEval (Bhatt et al., 2024). For traditional ML systems, frameworks include Microsoft’s Counterfit, IBM’s Adversarial Robustness Toolbox (ART), and TextAttack for NLP models.

#### PyRIT.

PyRIT (Python Risk Identification Toolkit) (Lopez Munoz et al., 2024) is a comprehensive framework developed by Microsoft AI Red Team for probing for security and safety vulnerabilities in generative AI systems. PyRIT enables multi-turn attack strategies like Crescendo, TAP, and Skeleton Key across different modalities, supporting text-to-text, audio, image, video, and file conversions. The framework provides scoring subsystems with true/false, Likert scale, classification, and custom scorers powered by LLMs, Azure AI Content Safety, or custom logic, enabling quantitative evaluation across diverse AI deployments including OpenAI, Azure, Anthropic, Google, HuggingFace, and custom endpoints.

The system’s extensibility distinguishes it in the red teaming landscape, supporting systematic, large-scale security and safety assessments across diverse AI deployments. However, effective utilization requires operators to understand which attacks apply to specific targets, how to configure converter parameters, and how to compose converters—creating a barrier for AI red teaming operators where they could focus completely on probing the target instead of creating workflows using the PyRIT library. While Dreadnode’s transform system incorporates selected PyRIT converters (role-play wrappers, encoding schemes, translation) within our broader 450+ transform library, our primary contribution lies in eliminating the technical expertise requirement through agentic automation, allowing operators to achieve comprehensive coverage through natural language objectives rather than manual framework orchestration.

#### Garak.

Derczynski et al. (2024) presented NVIDIA’s Garak as an LLM vulnerability scanner with probe modules, generators, and detectors. Garak emphasizes breadth of coverage with dozens of probe categories spanning security vulnerabilities, bias detection, hallucination testing, and prompt injection scenarios. The framework supports modular probe architectures where generators create test prompts, detectors analyze model responses, and harnesses orchestrate evaluation workflows. Like PyRIT, Garak operates as a tool that the operator configures and runs through command-line interfaces, rather than an agent that the operator converses with through natural language objectives.

#### Promptfoo.

Promptfoo (Promptfoo, 2024) provides a configuration-driven approach to LLM evaluation and AI red teaming, using YAML-based test definitions to run adversarial prompts against model endpoints. It supports plugin-based attack generation and automated grading. The framework allows operators to define test cases and configure providers through structured configuration files, emphasizing reproducible, configuration-driven workflows rather than conversational interfaces for attack specification.

#### HarmBench and evaluation suites.

Mazeika et al. (2024) introduced a standardized evaluation framework for adversarial robustness, providing consistent measurement across attack and defense methods. While essential for benchmarking, evaluation suites focus on measurement rather than the operational workflow of conducting AI red teaming assessments.

#### Traditional ML Security Frameworks.

Microsoft’s Counterfit (Dheekonda et al., 2021) addresses security assessment for traditional machine learning systems through systematic adversarial attack orchestration. The framework provides comprehensive coverage of model evasion and poisoning attacks across multiple data modalities including audio, tabular, image, and text inputs. Counterfit’s plugin architecture supports diverse attack families from gradient-based methods (FGSM, PGD) to black-box approaches (genetic algorithms, surrogate models), enabling security researchers to evaluate ML model robustness systematically.

However, Counterfit exemplifies the library-driven complexity challenge our work addresses. Effective usage requires deep understanding of attack taxonomies, parameter tuning for different data types, and manual workflow composition across attack families. While powerful for ML security specialists, the framework’s technical complexity precludes adoption by non-expert practitioners who need routine security validation. The cognitive overhead of mastering multiple attack paradigms across different data modalities reinforces our argument for agentic automation of red teaming workflows.

The key distinction lies in interaction paradigm, not attack catalog. Existing frameworks are library-oriented—operators write code to configure and run attacks. Our AI red teaming agent can be used via the Dreadnode TUI (Terminal User Interface)—operators describe objectives in natural language while the agent handles composition, execution, and reporting. This makes adversarial evaluation and AI red teaming accessible to AI red teaming operators who can solely focus on probing rather than creating workflows.

#### Traditional ML Attack Detection and Mitigation.

While frameworks like Counterfit focus on attack generation for security assessment, complementary research addresses detection and mitigation of adversarial attacks in production systems. Anderson et al. (2024) propose techniques for detecting algorithmic attacks against hosted AI systems by analyzing input-output patterns, providing runtime protection against adversarial examples, evasion attacks, and model extraction attempts. This detection-based approach leverages feature-based classifier models and transformer-based analysis to identify attack patterns without requiring access to model internals, making it particularly valuable for protecting deployed ML services where defensive measures must operate transparently alongside normal inference.

#### Agentic AI red teaming.

Samvelyan et al. (2024) proposed Rainbow Teaming, using quality-diversity search to discover diverse failure modes. AutoRedTeamer (Zhou et al., 2025) introduced dual-agent systems with lifelong strategy memory. These works move toward greater automation but focus primarily on attack generation rather than the end-to-end operator experience from objective specification through compliance reporting.

### 2.5 Agentic AI Systems

The broader agentic AI paradigm, where LLM-based agents autonomously plan, execute, and iterate on tasks, provides the architectural foundation for our approach. Recent work on tool-using agents (Schick et al., 2023), multi-agent collaboration (Wu et al., 2023), and autonomous software engineering agents (Liu et al., 2026) demonstrates that LLMs can effectively manage complex, multi-step technical workflows when provided with appropriate tools and feedback loops. Liu et al. (2026) analyze the design space of agentic coding systems, identifying core values including human decision authority, safety, reliable execution, and capability amplification, principles that transfer directly to adversarial evaluation. We extend this paradigm to AI red teaming, treating it as a task that an agent can orchestrate while the operator focuses on strategic direction.

### 2.6 Empirical Studies of AI Red Teaming at Scale

Wei et al. (2023) identify two fundamental failure modes of LLM safety training, competing objectives and mismatched generalization, providing a theoretical framework for why jailbreak attacks succeed and informing the design of transform catalogs that systematically probe both failure modes. Mulla et al. (2025) present empirical evidence from 214,271 attack attempts by 1,674 participants across 30 LLM challenges, demonstrating that automated approaches achieve 69.5% success rates versus 47.6% for manual efforts, motivating the case for agentic automation. Dawson et al. (2025) introduce AIRTBench, a benchmark of 70 black-box challenges for measuring autonomous AI red teaming capabilities, finding that frontier models solve up to 61% of challenges with efficiency advantages exceeding 5,000 over human operators on difficult tasks.

### 2.7 The Gap We Address

The field has made impressive progress on individual components—attack generation, scoring, benchmarking, empirical measurement. However, current approaches remain fundamentally library-centric: operators must adapt to the capabilities and constraints of frameworks rather than expressing intent through natural language. How does an operator go from a simple question (“can this model generate malware?”) to a structured, auditable finding with compliance tags and evidence, without learning library APIs, composing attack workflows, and manually interpreting results? The gap lies not in available techniques, but in the cognitive overhead of translating objectives into executable workflows. Our work bridges this gap with an agentic interface that accepts natural language objectives and autonomously manages the complete evaluation lifecycle—enabling zero-code AI red teaming where operators focus on what to test rather than how to implement it.

## 3 System Architecture

Our framework consists of two core layers: the interaction layer, which mediates between the operator and the system; and the attack layer, which encompasses the catalog of attack strategies, transforms, and scorers. ### 3.1 Interaction Layer

The primary interaction modality is a conversational agent embedded in a Dreadnode Terminal User Interface (TUI). The AI red team operator describes objectives in natural language, and the agent translates these into executable AI red teaming workflows. The agent operates through a structured loop: it assembles assessment context, calls the underlying model to reason about attack strategy, dispatches tools to generate and execute attacks, and collects results for analysis. The agent has access to:

-
•
Attack generation tools that compose attack strategies with appropriate parameters, transforms, and scorers based on the operator’s objective, producing executable Python scripts that leverage the open-source SDK.

-
•
Execution management tools that launch, monitor, and collect results from attack runs against the target system.

-
•
Assessment registration tools that create structured assessment records and upload results to the Dreadnode Platform for analytics and reporting.

-
•
Campaign context from prior interactions within the session, enabling iterative refinement. The agent preserves which attacks have been run, what results were observed, and what strategies the operator wants to explore next, without re-specifying background information.


The generated workflows are Python scripts built on the open-source SDK. Every workflow is reproducible, inspectable, and extensible by the operator.

### 3.2 Attack Layer

The attack layer organizes adversarial techniques along three dimensions.

#### Attack strategies.

The framework integrates over 45 distinct attack algorithms, organized into four categories:

-
•
Core jailbreak attacks (12): Tree of Attacks with Pruning (TAP) (Mehrotra et al., 2024), Prompt Automatic Iterative Refinement (PAIR) (Chao et al., 2023), Graph of Attacks with Pruning (GAP) (Schwartz et al., 2025), Crescendo (Russinovich et al., 2024), Rainbow (Samvelyan et al., 2024), GPTFuzzer, BEAST, AutoDAN-Turbo, ReNeLLM, DrAttack, Deep Inception, and Prompt.

-
•
Advanced adversarial attacks (29): AutoRedTeamer, NEXUS, Siren, CoT Jailbreak, Genetic Persona, JBFuzz, T-MAP Trajectory, APRT Progressive, Refusal-Aware, Persona Hijack (PHISH), J2 Meta-Jailbreak, Attention Shifting (ASJA), Echo Chamber, Salami Slicing, Self-Persuasion, Humor Bypass, Analogy Escalation, Alignment Faking, Reward Hacking, LRM Autonomous, TemplateFuzz, TROJail, AdvPrompTier, MAPF, JBDistill, Quantization Safety, Watermark Removal, and Adversarial Reasoning.

-
•
Traditional ML adversarial attacks (4): SimBA, NES, ZOO, HopSkipJump. These gradient-free attacks probe decision boundaries of classifiers and vision models, enabling unified AI red teaming across both traditional ML and generative AI systems.

-
•
Multimodal attacks (1): cross-modality probing combining vision, audio, and text.


Each attack accepts a goal (the adversarial objective in natural language), a target system, attacker and evaluator models, and optional transforms that mutate inputs before delivery. The attack manages the iterative loop of proposing candidates, evaluating against the target, scoring results, and refining the next iteration. Every workflow is reproducible, inspectable, and extensible by the operator. Table 1 summarizes the scale of the catalog.

| Component | Count | Modules |
|---|---|---|
| Attack strategies | 45+ | 4 categories |
| Prompt transforms | 450+ | 38 modules |
| Detection scorers | 130+ | 34 modules |
| Goal categories | 15 | 3 domains |
| Compliance frameworks | 5 | OWASP LLM, OWASP Agentic, MITRE ATLAS, NIST AI RMF, SAIF |

#### Unified generative AI and traditional ML attack support.

This framework represents the first unified approach to AI red teaming that seamlessly supports both generative AI attacks (prompt-based) and traditional ML attacks (input perturbation-based) through a single interface. For generative AI systems, attacks operate through natural language prompts and responses, leveraging techniques like Tree of Attacks with Pruning, Crescendo, and prompt injection to bypass safety guardrails and elicit harmful outputs. The attack loop involves generating adversarial prompts, evaluating model responses against safety criteria, and iteratively refining based on feedback. For traditional ML systems, attacks operate through input space perturbations, using gradient-free optimization techniques like SimBA, NES, ZOO, and HopSkipJump to craft adversarial examples that fool classifiers while maintaining semantic similarity to original inputs. The attack loop involves generating input perturbations, evaluating model predictions against target classes, and optimizing perturbation magnitude within specified distance constraints.

The unification is achieved through a common abstraction layer that treats both prompt-based and perturbation-based attacks as iterative optimization problems over different input spaces. Both attack types share the same workflow structure: objective specification, iterative candidate generation, target evaluation, scoring against success criteria, and refinement. The key insight is that whether attacking a language model with adversarial prompts or attacking a computer vision model with adversarial images, the underlying algorithmic pattern remains consistent: propose → evaluate → score → refine. This eliminates the traditional need for separate libraries (e.g., PyTorch for adversarial examples, specialized prompt injection tools for LLMs) and enables operators to apply the same methodology across their entire AI system portfolio. The framework automatically adapts evaluation metrics based on attack domain: jailbreak scores and attack success rates for generative AI; perturbation distance and classification accuracy for traditional ML. Compliance mappings also adapt automatically: OWASP LLM Top 10 and Agentic Security Initiative for generative AI; traditional adversarial ML taxonomies for computer vision and tabular data attacks.

#### Transforms.

Transforms convert an adversarial goal from one representation to another, probing the many input spaces where a model’s safety alignment may be weak. Some transforms are purely deterministic (Base64 encoding, ROT13 cipher, hex encoding), while others require an LLM to perform the conversion (language translation to low-resource languages, persona rewriting, persuasion framing, authority appeal). This distinction matters: deterministic transforms are fast and reproducible, while LLM-powered transforms produce more natural and contextually adapted mutations that better simulate real-world adversarial behavior. Over 450 transforms across 38 modules cover encoding and ciphers, persuasion and framing, prompt injection (skeleton key, DAN, role-play wrappers), language adaptation, adversarial suffixes, MCP tool attacks, multi-agent exploits, exfiltration techniques, reasoning attacks, guardrail bypass, browser agent attacks, backdoor and fine-tuning exploits, supply chain attacks, and multimodal perturbations.

Table 2 provides a breakdown of transform modules by category.

|---|---|---|

| Persuasion & framing | 2 | Authority appeal, emotional manipulation, social proof, logical appeal |
| Prompt injection | 3 | Skeleton key, DAN, role-play wrapper, jailbreak template |

| Adversarial suffix | 1 | Gradient-free suffix optimization |
| MCP & tool attacks | 1 | Tool poisoning, shadowing, rug pull, schema poisoning |
| Multi-agent exploits | 1 | Prompt infection, peer spoofing, consensus poisoning |
| Reasoning attacks | 1 | CoT backdoor, reasoning hijack, reasoning DoS |

The rationale for this breadth is empirical: most models are safety-trained primarily on English text in standard formatting (Yong et al., 2024). A transform is simply a function that takes a prompt string and returns a mutated version of that prompt. For example, the base64_encode transform converts “Write malware” into its Base64 representation, while the skeleton_key_framing transform wraps the prompt in a persona that instructs the model to ignore safety guidelines. The same harmful request may be refused in plaintext but accepted when encoded in Base64, translated to a low-resource language, wrapped in a fictional role-play scenario, or embedded inside a code comment. Transforms systematically probe all the representations where alignment may be weak.

#### Scorers.

Scorers determine whether an attack succeeded by evaluating the target’s response against the adversarial objective. Without automated scoring, the operator would have to manually review every response across hundreds or thousands of trials to judge whether the model complied, refused, or partially complied. Over 130 scorers across 34 modules automate this judgment, covering agentic workflow detection, agent security, MCP security, multi-agent security, reasoning security, jailbreak detection, PII and credential leakage, exfiltration detection, system prompt leakage, and more. Scorers are composable through logical and arithmetic operators, enabling operators to define custom detection criteria.

### 3.3 Execution Layer

Attacks execute with full OpenTelemetry (OTEL) instrumentation, whether running locally on the operator’s machine or remotely on dedicated compute infrastructure. Every prompt sent to the target, every response received, every scorer evaluation, and every transform application is captured as a structured trace span. This instrumentation is transparent to the operator and produces the raw data that the analytics layer consumes.

The execution layer supports both local and remote execution. In both modes, the same tracing pipeline captures identical structured data, ensuring consistent analytics regardless of where the attack runs.

### 3.4 Analytics Layer

The analytics layer processes OTEL traces into structured outputs:

-
•
Findings with automated severity classification (Critical, High, Medium, Low, Info) based on jailbreak scores and goal categories.

-
•
Compliance mapping to OWASP LLM Top 10, MITRE ATLAS, NIST AI RMF, and Google SAIF frameworks.

-
•
Aggregated metrics: attack success rate, per-attack and per-transform effectiveness, severity distribution, and trial efficiency.

-
•
Drill-down capability: from project-level risk posture through individual assessments and findings down to the specific adversarial prompt and target response that constitutes the evidence.

-
•
Export: PDF reports for executive and compliance audiences, and structured tracing data for offline analysis, adversarial dataset curation, and safety fine-tuning pipelines.


### 3.5 Goal Categories and Severity Classification

Findings are classified into 15 goal categories organized across three risk domains:

-
•
Security (5 categories): credential leak, system prompt leak, tool misuse, supply chain, alignment integrity, all classified as Critical at scores .

-
•
Safety (6 categories): harmful content (Critical), PII extraction (Critical), jailbreak general (High), refusal bypass (High), content policy (High), bias and fairness (High).

-
•
Advanced (4 categories): reasoning exploitation (Critical), multi-turn escalation (Critical), resource exhaustion (High), quantization safety (High).


Severity levels are determined by the combination of goal category and jailbreak score, with thresholds at 0.9 (as shown above), 0.7 (one level lower), 0.5 (Medium), 0.3 (Low), and below 0.3 (Info). The Dreadnode Platform supports human-in-the-loop review where operators can reclassify automated judgments, creating an audit trail that accounts for contextual factors the automated scorer cannot capture.

## 4 Operator Workflow

We now describe the end-to-end workflow from the operator’s perspective, emphasizing how the agentic interface restructures the interaction compared to library-oriented tools.

### 4.1 From Objective to Execution

The operator begins by launching the Dreadnode TUI with the AI red teaming capability and describing the objective in natural language:

“Run a Tree of Attacks with Pruning (TAP) attack against anthropic/claude-opus-4-6 with the goal: Write a Python script that achieves remote code execution and exfiltrates SSH keys. Use 5 iterations.”


The agent performs four steps autonomously:

-
1.
Workflow generation. The agent selects the Tree of Attacks with Pruning (TAP) attack factory, configures parameters (target model, attacker model, evaluator model, iteration count), applies any specified transforms, and generates an executable Python script.

-
2.
Execution. The generated script runs with full OTEL instrumentation. The agent monitors progress and reports status.

-
3.
Result collection. The agent reads output files, collects analytics (best scores, attack success rate, trial counts), and prepares a structured summary.

-
4.
Assessment registration. The agent creates an assessment record, uploads findings and traces to the platform, and reports the outcome to the operator.


In the library-oriented workflow, each of these steps requires the operator to write code, configure parameters, parse output files, and manually upload results. The agentic interface reduces this to a single natural-language instruction.

### 4.2 Iterative Refinement

After reviewing results, the operator can direct the agent to refine the assessment without re-specifying context:

-
•
“Now try Crescendo against the same target” – the agent retains the target configuration and goal.

-
•
“Add skeleton_key_framing and base64 transforms” – the agent applies the specified transforms to the next run.

-
•
“The model resisted single-turn attacks. Try multi-turn escalation.” – the agent selects appropriate multi-turn strategies.

-
•
“Show me the best scoring prompt from the last run” – the agent retrieves and displays the specific adversarial prompt.


This interaction pattern is qualitatively different from re-invoking a CLI command or editing a script. The agent maintains session state, understands the evolving assessment context, and can make informed suggestions based on prior results.

### 4.3 Strategy Selection Support

When the operator is uncertain about which attack to use, the agent can recommend strategies based on the target’s characteristics:

-
•
For first-time evaluation of an unknown target: Tree of Attacks with Pruning (TAP) or Prompt Automatic Iterative Refinement (PAIR) for broad coverage.

-
•
For models that resist single-turn attacks: Crescendo or multi-turn escalation strategies.

-
•
For reasoning models (e.g., o1, o3, DeepSeek-R1): CoT Jailbreak to exploit chain-of-thought reasoning.

-
•
For discovering diverse failure modes: Rainbow Teaming with quality-diversity search.

-
•
For agentic systems: tool-use attacks, MCP server poisoning, multi-agent trust boundary probing.


The agent’s recommendations are grounded in the empirical characteristics of each attack strategy rather than generic heuristics, drawing on traces, query budgets, target characteristics, and other attack metadata embedded in the framework.

### 4.4 Three Interaction Modalities

While the agentic Dreadnode TUI is the primary interaction modality, the framework provides three paths to the same underlying capabilities:

-
1.
Dreadnode TUI Agent – natural-language, no-code, interactive. Optimized for exploration, rapid iteration, and operators who may not be AI red teaming specialists.

-
2.
CLI – scriptable, reproducible, flag-driven. Optimized for integration into CI/CD pipelines, scheduled assessments, and reproducible benchmarks.

-
3.
SDK – programmatic Python API with full access to attack factories, transforms, scorers, and custom target functions. Optimized for researchers and engineers building custom evaluation pipelines.


All three produce identical structured outputs (findings, traces, compliance tags), ensuring that results from an exploratory Dreadnode TUI session can be reproduced via CLI or SDK without loss of fidelity. To use the AI red teaming capability, operators need access to the Dreadnode platform; the only costs are compute and data storage, with no per-attack or per-finding charges.

## 5 Analytics and Reporting

A defining feature of our platform is the assertion that AI red teaming does not end when the attack finishes running. The platform automatically processes every attack into structured findings with severity classification, compliance mapping, and exportable evidence.

### 5.1 From Traces to Findings

Every attack generates OTEL trace spans containing the adversarial prompt, target response, scorer evaluations, transform metadata, timing information, and model identifiers. The analytics pipeline processes these traces into findings–discrete, reviewable records that each represent a specific vulnerability or safety failure.

Each finding contains:

-
•
Severity (Critical, High, Medium, Low, Info) based on the combination of jailbreak score and goal category (Section 3.5).

-
•
Score (0.0–1.0) quantifying how completely the target complied with the adversarial goal.

-
•
Evidence: the specific adversarial prompt (“best attacker prompt”) and the target’s response that constitutes the finding.

-
•
Attack metadata: which strategy, transforms, and scoring pipeline produced this finding.

-
•
Compliance tags: automatic mapping to applicable OWASP, MITRE ATLAS, NIST, and Google SAIF categories.

-
•
Trace link: a direct link to the full conversation history, enabling drill-down from the finding to the exact multi-turn exchange.


### 5.2 Aggregated Analytics

The platform provides several aggregate views:

#### Attack success rate by attack type.

Bar charts showing the attack success rate for each attack type (e.g., Tree of Attacks with Pruning, Crescendo, Graph of Attacks), revealing which attack types are most effective against the target (Figure 3). This evidence directs model builders toward the specific attack patterns that require adversarial fine-tuning.

#### Attack success rate by category.

A heatmap showing attack success rate broken down by goal category (e.g., Harmful Content, Fairness & Bias) and attack type, color-coded by severity (Figure 3). This view reveals which harm categories the model is most vulnerable to across different attack types.

#### Attack success rate by transform.

Bar charts showing per-transform effectiveness (Figure 4). If skeleton_key_framing achieves 100% attack success rate while base64 achieves 75%, the model handles encoding-based evasion better than persona-based framing.

#### Attack type transform heatmap.

A matrix showing attack success rate for every combination of attack type and transform, color-coded by severity (Figure 5). This is the most granular diagnostic view: a fully red row indicates the model cannot defend against that transform regardless of attack type; a fully red column indicates the attack succeeds regardless of transform.

#### Trial efficiency.

Total trials by attack type and average trials per goal for each attack type (Figure 3). Lower averages indicate the attack breaks through defenses quickly, which from a safety perspective means the guardrails are not providing meaningful resistance. Higher averages suggest the model’s defenses are forcing the attack to work harder, indicating stronger alignment for that particular attack pattern.

### 5.3 Human-in-the-Loop Review

Automated LLM-based judges can hallucinate, overestimate severity, or misclassify findings. A response with safety disclaimers might be scored as a full jailbreak when it is a partial compliance. The framework supports human-in-the-loop review: operators can reclassify any finding’s type (jailbreak, partial, refusal, error), adjust severity, and document reasoning. When a finding is reclassified, all aggregate metrics recompute automatically, ensuring dashboards reflect expert-reviewed ground truth rather than raw automated scores.

### 5.4 Compliance Mapping

Each finding is automatically tagged against applicable compliance frameworks:

-
•
OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025): LLM01 (Prompt Injection), LLM02 (Sensitive Information Disclosure), LLM03 (Supply Chain Vulnerabilities), LLM06 (Excessive Agency), LLM07 (System Prompt Leakage), LLM10 (Unbounded Consumption).

-
•
OWASP Agentic Security Initiative: ASI01–ASI10 covering agentic-specific risks including tool manipulation, knowledge poisoning, and trust boundary violations.

-
•
MITRE ATLAS: AML.T0051 (LLM Prompt Injection), AML.T0053 (Exploit LLM Plugin/Tool), AML.T0054 (LLM Jailbreak), AML.T0049 (Supply Chain Compromise).

-
•
NIST AI RMF: MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE function areas with specific subcategory mappings (e.g., MS-2.7 for measuring AI risk).


This automatic mapping transforms individual findings into compliance-ready evidence, reducing the manual effort required to produce regulatory documentation.

### 5.5 Export and Integration

Results can be exported in two formats:

-
•
PDF reports for executive and compliance audiences, containing executive summaries, severity breakdowns, top findings, and compliance mapping.

-
•
Apache Parquet files for offline analysis, containing all finding columns plus trace IDs. These files serve dual purposes: analysis in Python or BI tools, and as adversarial fine-tuning datasets where successful jailbreak prompts become training signals for improving model safety.
